articles.title_orig: Wendy's rejects buyout bid from activist investor and adopts 'poison pill' plan - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Wendy's rejects buyout bid from activist investor and adopts 'poison pill' plan - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Wendy’s rejected a $1.4 billion buyout offer from an activist investor, saying Thursday that the bid was too low
Wendy’s rejected a $1.4 billion buyout offer from an activist investor, saying Thursday that the bid was too low, and it adopted a “poison pill” plan that would make it more difficult to engineer a hostile takeover of the company.
Noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer last week to buy the chain, which has been struggling with high beef prices and aging stores. Peltz said the fast-food landscape had become increasingly challenging, with consumers under pressure, intensifying competition and persistent inflation, and his offer was the best path forward for shareholders.
But in a conference call with investors Thursday, Wendy's CEO Bob Wright, who joined the company in May from Potbelly, said Wendy's has a turnaround plan in place that is already producing good results.
“We’re confident that we have the right strategy, execution and resources to restore Wendy’s to its full potential and drive meaningful shareholder value,” Wright said.
Shares rose more than 2% Thursday as the company reported a better than expected performance during the third quarter.
Wendy's said in a statement that a committee of independent directors unanimously rejected the offer because it “substantially undervalues” the company.
Wendy's also announced that it has adopted a shareholders' rights plan, a so-called “poison pill,” intended to avert a hostile takeover of the company. The plan, which grants all shareholders except the hostile bidder the right to purchase discounted shares, automatically triggers if a person or group owns 15% or more of Wendy's shares.
Peltz's Trian Fund Management and other partners in the investor group that made the offer to Wendy's hold 16.3% of the company's shares. The plan would stay in place for one year, Wendy's said. Trian didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Wendy’s has been closing outdated U.S. restaurants so it can focus on its more profitable locations. The company closed 240 restaurants in 2024 and said earlier this year that it planned to shutter up to 358 locations in 2026.
Then, in September, one of the largest U.S. franchisees for Wendy’s filed for bankruptcy protection after the chain tried to terminate its franchise agreement. Michigan-based Meritage Hospitality Group operates 314 Wendy’s restaurants in 15 states.
Wendy’s, which is based in Dublin, Ohio, had 5,969 restaurants in the U.S. and 1,428 outlets in 38 countries at the end of 2025.
Founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas and named after his daughter, Wendy's is known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts. The fast-growing chain introduced the drive-thru window in 1970 and went public in 1976. In the 1980s, as it jockeyed for sales with McDonald’s and Burger King, Wendy’s launched salad bars and ran its iconic “Where’s the beef?” ad campaign.
But as the fast-food market grew even more competitive and rival burger-focused chains like In-N-Out and Five Guys expanded, Wendy’s fell behind. Wendy’s share of U.S. burger chain sales fell from 11.5% in 2019 to 10.4% last year, according to Technomic, a market research company.

articles.title_orig: Oman Sultan, Iran and Saudi envoys visit China
articles.title_zh: Oman Sultan, Iran and Saudi envoys visit China
articles.content_orig:
At the invitation of President Xi Jinping, Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik Al Said of Oman paid a state visit to China from November 1 to 2. This was the first China visit by an Omani head of state since diplomatic ties were established 48 years ago in 1978.
Ding Long, a professor at the Middle East Studies Institute of Shanghai International Studies University, told Global Times that with tensions mounting in the Strait of Hormuz, and Oman, which has been a long-standing active mediator in regional disputes, coming under pressure as well, the visit reflects the country’s efforts to strengthen strategic support and enhance diplomatic autonomy.
Oman is the only member of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) to consistently maintain positive relations with Iran, and it has played a pivotal role in regional diplomacy, including hosting rounds of talks between Iran and the United States. Its peaceful policy has earned at least one threat from US President Donald Trump to bomb the country.
Chinese President Xi Jinping held talks with Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik Al Said on November 2. He said that China stands ready to work with Oman to steer their strategic partnership to a higher level, and to help restore peace and realise lasting stability in the Middle East at an early date. China and Oman, he added, should enhance political mutual trust and strengthen exchanges of experience in national governance, while expressing China’s support for Oman in safeguarding national independence, sovereignty, security and stability, and in independently exploring a development path suited to its national conditions. And China, he said, is ready to deepen the synergy of development strategies with Oman and to be a stable and reliable partner in the energy sector, a partner with promising potential in investment, and a partner in fostering innovation in advanced technologies.
“China has been actively committed to ending hostilities and promoting peace, aiming to contribute its wisdom and solutions to resolving the regional security predicament,” Xi said, adding that China will continue to advocate resolving disputes through political and diplomatic means, and support regional countries in building a common home of good-neighbourliness, development, security and cooperation.
Stressing that China has been Oman’s largest trading partner for many years and Chinese enterprises’ investment in Oman has kept growing, Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik said his country is ready to synergise development strategies with China and strengthen cooperation in trade, investment, industry, infrastructure, AI, science and technology, and other fields. He said Oman highly appreciates China’s just position on the Middle East issue and stands ready to maintain close coordination with China to uphold international law, advocate for the peaceful resolution of disputes, and jointly promote security and stability in the region and beyond.
Later that day, Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik met with Chinese Premier Li Qiang. Li said the talks between the two heads of state earlier that morning mapped out a new blueprint for further deepening the China-Oman strategic partnership. He expressed China’s willingness to strengthen the alignment of development strategies with Oman, deepen cooperation across the entire oil and gas industry chain, and carry out more high-quality clean energy projects and called on both sides to expand cooperation in areas such as agriculture and fisheries, aerospace satellites, information and communication, and artificial intelligence, and promote the early conclusion of the free trade agreement negotiations between China and the GCC. He stressed that China and Oman, both Global South countries, should maintain close communication and coordination in multilateral affairs to jointly safeguard world peace and stability.
Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik said Oman deeply admires China’s development achievements, which have attracted attention worldwide. Oman looks forward to learning from China’s development experience and deepening mutually beneficial cooperation between the two countries. Oman is willing to enhance communication and coordination with China in international and regional affairs and to contribute to resolving conflicts and maintaining peace and stability in the Middle East and the Gulf region.
In a potentially significant but under-reported related development, also on November 2, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met separately with the Deputy Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council and the National Security Advisor of Saudi Arabia.
Meeting with Deputy Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Ali Bagheri Kani, Wang Yi stated that China-Iran relations have maintained steady development despite a volatile international landscape. This serves the fundamental interests of both peoples and reflects the aspirations of Global South countries for solidarity and cooperation. China supports Iran in safeguarding its sovereignty and security and is willing to work with Iran to further advance bilateral relations.
Ali Bagheri Kani briefed Wang Yi on Iran’s views concerning the regional situation, stating that Iran would firmly safeguard its security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, and resist power politics and threats. Iran is also willing to engage in talks and negotiations with all parties and work actively for regional peace and stability. The Iranian side appreciates the initiatives and proposals put forward by President Xi Jinping and China’s consistent commitment to multilateralism. Iran looks forward to China playing a greater role in international and regional peace. Iran stands ready to promote the steady development of bilateral ties and to strengthen cooperation with China in international and multilateral frameworks.
In his meeting with Wang Yi, Saudi Arabia’s Minister of State, Member of the Council of Ministers, and National Security Advisor Musaad bin Mohammed Al-Aiban handed over a letter from Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman to President Xi Jinping regarding the development of China-Saudi bilateral relations and issues of mutual concern.
Wang Yi said that the current regional situation has once again reached a critical crossroads between war and peace. Although the road to peace is not smooth, it is necessary to keep moving forward. He hoped that all parties would resolve disputes and end the conflict through dialogue and negotiation, safeguarding regional energy and shipping security. China believes that countries in the region should enhance understanding, rebuild mutual trust, improve relations, and live harmoniously, promoting the construction of a new regional security framework that serves the long-term interests of their peoples through consultation.

articles.title_orig: Dow plunges 1,200 points, shedding most of midterm results stock rally - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Dow plunges 1,200 points, shedding most of midterm results stock rally - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The selloff came a day after the Dow soared more than 1,500 points.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged about 1,200 points on Thursday, eroding most of the rally from a day earlier when midterm election results propelled the index to its best trading session in more than a year.
The S & P 500 dropped 3.2%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 4.8%, putting the index into correction territory, meaning it has fallen more than 10% from a previous peak last month.
The Dow declined 1,220 points, or 2.2%.
The selloff hammered many artificial intelligence firms as investors appeared to digest risk for the sector posed by newly empowered Democrats, many of whom ran campaigns critical of artificial intelligence data centers.
Nvidia, the chipmaking giant behind many of the semiconductors used in AI products, dropped 7% on Thursday. Rival chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices saw shares fall 12%. SanDisk, another AI hardware firm, plummeted more than 15% in value.
The slide also hit some other major tech firms behind AI development.
Microsoft, which holds a large stake in OpenAI, saw its stock price fall more than 2%. Amazon, which has spent hundreds of billions on its build-out of AI infrastructure, also dropped more than 2%.
The downturn in markets largely reversed blockbuster gains from the previous session.
On Wednesday, the Dow jumped 1,570 points, or 3%, recording its best one-day performance since April 9, 2025, when President Donald Trump announced the suspension of a far-reaching set of reciprocal tariffs.
Even as stocks climbed on Wednesday, Yorkville analyst Dan Ives warned ABC News of potential midterm fallout for the tech sector.
"The Democratic blue tidal wave across the Senate and House was a seismic shift that will have a negative impact on the pace of the AI Revolution buildout in the US over the next few years," Ives told ABC News in a statement.
Tuesday's midterm elections catapulted Democratic Senate and gubernatorial candidates to statewide victories in Republican strongholds like Ohio and Texas, both of which play host to a number of AI data centers.
A strong performance in House contests, meanwhile, appeared to set Democrats on a path toward a comfortable majority in the lower chamber.
OpenAI unveiled a new set of data center policies Thursday for that it called "responsible AI infrastructure" in the aftermath of the election.
The ChatGPT maker said it would abide by fresh commitments, including a vow to pay for all electricity and infrastructure used at its facilities. It also will create a "water plan" for each location as part of an effort to "protect local resources," and will "create opportunities for local workers and businesses" for employment, the AI company said in a blog post .

articles.title_orig: Xbox overhauls its PC, web, and cloud apps with a faster design
articles.title_zh: Xbox overhauls its PC, web, and cloud apps with a faster design
articles.content_orig:
Xbox Insiders can start testing the new PC app today.
Xbox Insiders can start testing the new PC app today.
Microsoft is unveiling a new Xbox PC app that launches “up to 60 percent faster” than before, with an overhauled design to match new updates to Xbox Cloud Gaming on the web and smart TVs. Xbox Insiders will be able to start testing the updated Xbox PC app today, and the updated Xbox Cloud Gaming interface will start rolling out over the next few weeks.
Ever since Microsoft launched its Xbox Ally handheld devices last year, it was clear the Xbox PC app still needed a lot of work to feel more like an Xbox console experience on Windows. Microsoft has greatly simplified the app now, with a design that no longer feels like you’re clicking a mouse when you’re using a controller.
“The app now launches up to 60 percent faster,” says Jason Beaumont , VP of Xbox experiences. “Pages like Home, Store, and Game Pass load up to 50 percent faster, and in-app windows open up to 65 percent faster.” The Xbox PC app also has simplified navigation that should make it easier to use on a controller, and the library section now has updated filters and better ways to organize your installed games.
Microsoft has improved the social parts of the Xbox PC app, too, with friends now listed in the main page and quick buttons to start a chat or join a party. The app overall feels less like a web one now, with what appears to be a mix of native and web elements. Microsoft has also refreshed the game card UI, as well as the home and settings sections. Even the animations have been updated to make this feel more like an Xbox dashboard experience.
I’ve been using this new Xbox PC app for the past few weeks, and it’s noticeably faster on a variety of devices I own. I’ve found it’s much easier to navigate around with a controller, and the search interface no longer tries to pop up when you’re moving between sections.
This redesign does make the Game Bar interface on handhelds feel a little out of place now, though. I understand Microsoft is looking to improve that in the coming months, and there should be design updates to make it match more closely to this updated Xbox PC app.
This new UI is also coming to Xbox Cloud Gaming. “We’re also bringing the refreshed Xbox web experience to more players and rolling out updates to Xbox Cloud Gaming apps on supported TVs and VR headsets,” says Beaumont. “These changes are part of our work to make Xbox faster, simpler, and more familiar wherever you play.”
The refreshed web version of Xbox Cloud Gaming has a similar look and feel to the Xbox PC app. A new library tab highlights cloud games across your own library and Xbox Game Pass. A desktop mode makes better use of larger displays, and you can choose between dark and light modes, as well as five new high-contrast options designed to improve accessibility support.
A similar design will also be available on smart TVs and VR headsets soon, but these designs aren’t exactly the same across PC, web, and smart TVs as Microsoft has customized them. “Playing on a PC, TV, or VR headset is different, and each experience needs to work well for the screen you’re using,” says Beaumont. “Wherever you play, the basics should feel familiar: finding your games, knowing what you can play, and getting into a game quickly.”

articles.title_orig: Tech stocks plunge on worries about AI and Democrats’ midterm landslide
articles.title_zh: Tech stocks plunge on worries about AI and Democrats’ midterm landslide
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman unseats Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, another win for the left in a major city
Shares in technology companies dropped sharply Thursday, compounding recent declines and sparking concerns about the durability of an artificial intelligence boom that has driven much of recent U.S. economic growth.
The tech-focused Nasdaq 100 index dropped as much as 6.2%, before rebounding to trade lower by about 4.5% throughout the late morning.
The S&P 500 also rebounded from earlier losses, but was still down 3.1%, putting it on track for its worst day since April 2025, when President Donald Trump’s global tariffs rocked markets.
The broader Nasdaq Composite, which tracks more than just tech stocks, also entered “correction” territory on Thursday, which is when a stock or index declines at least 10%.
Tech stocks have surged in recent years as excitement about artificial intelligence has fueled billions of dollars in investments in, and by, the companies that make chips and infrastructure necessary for AI’s development and operation.
Since Election Day 2024, the Nasdaq has surged almost 40%.
But questions about whether AI will enable the kind of productivity necessary to generate returns on those investments have grown louder in recent months.
“I don’t think this is an AI bubble bursting,” said Ed Yardeni, longtime market watcher and president of Yardeni Research. “I think it’s an AI bubble losing some air very, very rapidly, and I think that reduces the likelihood that we’ll get a bursting  bubble that has adverse consequences for the economy and broader financial system.”
Also contributing to losses were the commanding Democratic victories across the country in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Numerous Democrats who won races for governor, attorney general and Senate and House seats have pledged to slow or halt the construction of AI data centers.
Texas, Ohio, Michigan and Georgia were of particular concern, because they are all large data center markets.
“Today is the cold shower that I anticipated might occur after a blue-wave situation,” Yardeni said.
Elon Musk’s companies SpaceX and Tesla each slid nearly 10%, largely in response to the midterm results. But the two companies are also engaged in developing AI, and SpaceX has recently emerged as a data center developer.
Musk, the world’s first trillionaire, spent hundreds of millions to help elect Republican midterm candidates. Until Tuesday’s rout, he was seen as one of the largest potential beneficiaries of Republican victories.
Now that voters have so resoundingly rejected the GOP, Musk and his companies face the prospect of tighter regulation and even potential investigations at both the state and federal levels.
The sell-off was triggered by two lackluster earnings reports from major chipmakers, Qualcomm and Arm Holdings, which were released on Wednesday night. Both companies posted results that investors generally viewed as mixed.
The two companies were among the worst performers on the Nasdaq indexes, sliding 12%.
Earnings reports like these have rattled investors in recent months because of the hundreds of billions of dollars that are being poured into the AI sector.
Memory and chip firms SanDisk, Western Digital, AMD, Seagate and Micron were among the S&P 500’s biggest losers, all plunging around around 15%.
Oil prices rebounded from Wednesday’s drop. As of midmorning trading, Brent and U.S. crude oil rose 2%.
U.S. Treasury yields, which have faced some competition from tech giants tapping the bond markets to raise funds for their AI ambitions, were slightly lower.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped more than 1,250 points. The biggest contributor to the Dow’s drop was Nvidia, which sold off by 7%, its largest one-day decline since April 2025.
Nvidia is the most important supplier to any AI firm, but as investors raise questions about returns, the euphoria in the industry is fading. Nvidia’s shares have tanked 15% over the past three months.
Major established cloud computing providers Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft also fell, but less than the overall market declines.
Dow components Cisco and Caterpillar, which are both major suppliers to AI data centers, also dropped around 5%.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.
Allie Canal is a business reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia has lost nearly $1.4 trillion since its October record
articles.title_zh: Nvidia has lost nearly $1.4 trillion since its October record
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia ( NVDA ) is on track for its fifth straight losing week, and the slide since its October record has now erased nearly $1.4 trillion in market value.
Thursday did a lot of the damage. At its morning low, Nvidia was down more than 9%, knocking nearly $450 billion off its market value in a matter of hours and leaving the company worth about $4.4 trillion. A close there would be the stock's worst day since the DeepSeek sell-off in January 2025.
Nvidia has plenty of company.
AMD ( AMD ), Micron ( MU ), and Arm ( ARM ) are posting steep double-digit losses, and Broadcom ( AVGO ) and Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ) are falling near 10%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) is now more than a third below its June record.
Nvidia itself is down nearly 25% from its Oct. 6 record close and trading below its 200-day moving average .
The trigger this time is Washington. Democrats won both chambers of Congress, and candidates in both parties campaigned against AI data centers , the buildings that run on Nvidia's chips. The Senate came close to passing a bill this fall that would have made data centers pay more of the power costs they create.
Losing streaks this long don't come often for Nvidia. Since its 1999 IPO, the stock has strung together five or more down weeks just 12 times before this one. The longest ran seven weeks, in the summer of 2008.
The last one is the streak bulls will want to remember. It ended in October 2022, about a month before ChatGPT's launch set off the AI boom, and Nvidia's stock roughly quadrupled over the following year.
That's the best case, not the base case. Nvidia was higher 13 weeks later in only five of the 12 earlier streaks, though it was up a year later in eight. The worst came in 2002, when the stock lost nearly two-thirds of its value over the following year.
For now, Washington is the new worry hanging over the stock.
"There will be congressional hearings," Stifel's Brian Gardner told Reuters ahead of the vote. "There will be investigations."

articles.title_orig: Bank of England Raises Rates for First Time in Three Years
articles.title_zh: Bank of England Raises Rates for First Time in Three Years
articles.content_orig:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in three years as it warned that inflation is surging towards 5pc.
Policymakers voted to raise rates to 4pc from 3.75pc on Thursday in the first increase since August 2023.
The Bank blamed the ongoing conflict in the Middle East for triggering another sharp jump in energy prices, with John Healey’s maiden Budget doing little to ease a two-year decline in household incomes.
Threadneedle Street now believes inflation will peak around 5pc by the middle of 2027, even if the economy slows sharply.
However, policymakers said price rises would hit 6pc next summer if the Iran war drags on.
The Bank also laid bare the impact of the conflict on family finances, with Donald Trump’s war pushing up mortgage costs for the average household by £1,500.
The Ofgem energy price cap is now expected to rise by more than £400 to £2,150 in January, with the Chancellor’s £100 Budget handout doing little to mitigate the increase.
Andrew Bailey said growing price pressures from the prolonged war in Iran meant Thursday’s increase was unlikely to be the last.
Other members of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) raised the prospect of another rate rise before Christmas.
One member, Catherine Mann, called for an immediate 0.5 percentage point jump to 4.25pc.
Thanks for following our coverage of the Bank of England’s decision to raise interest rates for the first time in three years.
Andrew Bailey said there was a “strong” case for more rate rises as the Iran war ramps up inflation pressures on the economy.
You can keep up to date with the latest here .
Analysts at Goldman Sachs were surprised by the signals from the Bank of England that more interest rates were likely.
Andrew Bailey said he could “see the argument of a further increase in rates”, with fellow policymakers Clare Lombardelli, Huw Pill and Megan Greene also indicating further increases were on the cards.
The views of other rate setters also surprised Goldman.
James Moberly, an economist at the Wall Street bank, said: “We had not expected Catherine Mann to support a larger hike, and had anticipated that Alan Taylor and Swati Dhingra would prefer to hold.”
The FTSE 100 in London remains up 0.7pc despite the Bank of England signalling more interest rate rises could be on the way.
However, US tech stocks continued their falls this week in the wake of the midterm elections.
The Nasdaq Composite plunged 1.2pc to 25,427.44 at the open on Wall Street, while the benchmark S&P 500 fell 0.4pc to 7,654.89.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.5pc to 53,595.12 as investors switched out of tech stocks into more traditional sectors, over fears the Democrats would limit expansion of AI companies.
Traders expect too many interest rate rises from the Bank of England over the next year, an investment manager has warned.
April LaRusse, co-head of client portfolio management at BNY Investments, said money markets were anticipating too many further rate rises.
Traders are betting that the Bank will raise rates to 4.75pc by the end of next summer.
She said: “While we believe today’s increase was important in reinforcing the Bank’s inflation-fighting credibility, markets may now be somewhat too aggressive in the scale of further tightening they are pricing.
“Growth continues to benefit from strong business investment, particularly around AI-related infrastructure, but beyond this area we expect the economy to soften through 2027.
“Against that backdrop, the hurdle for further rate increases is likely to rise after the initial few hikes.”
Telegraph readers said inflation feels much more severe than the Bank of England’s forecasts of around 5pc in the early months of next year.
Here are some views from the comments section below and you can join the debate here .
Households face a “clear risk” that the Bank of England will raise interest rates in December after putting up borrowing costs for the first time in three years on Thursday.
Sanjay Raja, chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, said the “balance of risks has shifted” in favour of higher inflation, after policymakers forecast prices could rise at an annual pace of around 5pc early next year.
He said the latest rate rise was an “insurance policy” against the risk of inflation rising further and said he did not expect several increases in the future.
But he warned: “The bigger question from today’s decision is whether the next hike comes in December or February.
“There is a clear risk that the MPC could go earlier – this will be something to watch in the coming weeks and will likely be determined by forthcoming inflation outturns as well as developments in the Middle East (with the last 48 hours delivering some good news on energy price expectations).”
Andrew Bailey, coming towards the end of his press conference, said he hopes there will be more information on whether the Iran war will end by the Bank of England’s next meeting in December.
Answering a question from Telegraph economics editor Szu Ping Chan , he said: “We will judge this at each meeting.
“We will inevitably have more information by December because we will get more data releases and so on.
“I hope we will also have more information on where this conflict is going to. That would be the most important thing.”
Andrew Bailey said he “could see the case” for a further quarter point increase in interest rates to 4.25pc if the Middle East war is not resolved.
The Governor also said he would not sign up to suggestions that households faced just two rate rises as a result of the war.
“I’m not going to sign up to the two-and-done point,” he said.
Any further increase in interest rates would come down to “risk judgement”.
He said: “Things have happened in the last 48 hours but the whole situation is so volatile that we really don’t want to put much weight on two days, which frankly haven’t yet been backed by any firm evidence that there is a peace process which is going to lead to something concrete.”
Traders are betting it is a coin toss whether the Bank of England will raise interest rates for a second time before Christmas.
Money markets suggest there is a 53pc chance policymakers will vote for the Bank Rate to be lifted for a second meeting in a row to 4.25pc in December.
Traders had given a second rate rise this year a 30pc chance before the Bank announced it was raising rates from 3.75pc to 4pc.
However, they increased bets on higher rates after Andrew Bailey, the Governor, said there was a “strong” case for a second rate rise if the Iran war was not brought to an end.
John Healey has been urged to cut benefits and lower taxes after inflation rose to 4pc.
Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Rising interest rates are another headwind for hardworking families to deal with.
“They mean higher mortgage costs, and with the independent OBR confirming that living standards will fall next year, it’s time Labour cut taxes, welfare spending and costly regulations to make life cheaper for families.”
“The tax burden is expected to hit a record high in the wake of Mr Healey’s first Budget last week.”
Andrew Bailey called for an end to the Iran war to end the inflation pressure facing households this winter.
The Governor of the Bank of England said he was unable to tell people how high interest rates would go but said the best way to resolve price pressures in the economy was for the Middle East conflict to come to an end.
He said: “Inflation is bad for everybody... it is most difficult for those on low incomes and those struggling to find work.
“We are very conscious of the need to deal with this.
“In conditions that are as uncertain as the ones we face, I cannot give any assurances to people about where are interest rates going to go to.
“All I would come back to... and this was the same message as the Prime Minister gave yesterday, actually, which I firmly agree with, the focus must now be on dealing with this conflict, ending this conflict.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street Is Already Bracing for a 2027 Debt Ceiling Fight - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.title_zh: Wall Street Is Already Bracing for a 2027 Debt Ceiling Fight - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
America's billionaires woke up Wednesday to a political reckoning — and a Wall Street rally.
As Democrats celebrated a sweeping midterm victory , some of the country's wealthiest donors traded barbs over record election spending . Others warned the results could threaten the artificial intelligence boom.
Wall Street, however, cheered the outcome. The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared 1,569 points, or 3%, while the S&P 500 gained 1.6% and the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.4%, as investors welcomed political gridlock , reduced uncertainty and President Donald Trump's willingness to accept the results.
Virgin Group founder Richard Branson took aim at the billions spent influencing the election.
"I have felt embarrassed by the billions that tech entrepreneurs and hedge fund managers have spent," Branson wrote Wednesday on LinkedIn , calling for campaign finance reform. Branson did not give donations that met the reporting threshold in the 2026 election cycle.
His comments came as Elon Musk, the election's largest individual donor , watched his preferred Republicans lose the Texas Senate and governor races despite pouring $224 million into the state — nearly half his record $474 million in political giving nationwide, according to a CNBC analysis of campaign finance records.
Early Wednesday, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO suggested on X that data centers in space were looking increasingly appealing before joking that his "election-interfering space lasers" had failed.
LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman , another major political donor, took a sharper tone.
"We should get money out of politics," Hoffman wrote late Tuesday on X , accusing Musk of spending "outrageous amounts to keep authoritarian clowns in power" while defending his own contributions to Democrats.
Other Democratic megadonors celebrated. "The world changed yesterday," Alex Soros wrote Wednesday on X, hailing the results as a generational victory after his family contributed roughly $103 million to Democratic political efforts.
But beyond the political sparring, some of the country's richest investors were focused on a potentially bigger consequence of the Democratic sweep : the future of the AI boom .
Even before polls closed Tuesday, Pershing Square founder Bill Ackman warned on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that slowing AI development could jeopardize America's technological edge. "Practically speaking, we can't slow down," he said.
As results rolled in Tuesday night, billionaire investor Chamath Palihapitiya sounded an even starker warning.
Palihapitiya initially questioned whether the early results would hold, but warned that if they did, the implications for the AI trade could be severe.
"And the only way to sink the AI trade is to sink the data centers," Palihapitiya said during an election night livestream of the "All-In" podcast.
Texas offered an early test of those fears. Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, who has proposed a moratorium on new data center construction until stronger safeguards are established, defeated three-term Republican incumbent Greg Abbott.
During the same livestream, Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner warned the Democratic wave could mean at least 10 to 15 gigawatts of expected AI data center capacity would not come online in 2027. Wall Street analyst Dan Ives estimated Wednesday that 10% of planned U.S. data centers would no longer go ahead.
Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su acknowledged the growing resistance to AI's expansion , urging technology companies to demonstrate the benefits of data centers to local communities.
"At the end of the day, what we need to do is ensure that everybody wins from AI," Su told CNBC on Wednesday .
Yet Wall Street may have found opportunity in the same slowdown that worried AI's biggest backers.
Fewer new data centers could increase the value of existing facilities while easing the enormous spending burden on technology giants. Big Tech stocks surged Wednesday , adding more than $750 billion in market value at one point, even as smaller, debt-dependent data center operators tumbled.

articles.title_orig: Tankers hit in Hormuz as Iran keeps up pressure after US vote
articles.title_zh: Tankers hit in Hormuz as Iran keeps up pressure after US vote
articles.content_orig:
By The Maritime Executive 2026-11-04 14:45:03
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy continues to issue reports of multiple tankers being struck each day in the Strait of Hormuz. The latest reports came hours after the results of the U.S. midterm elections were emerging and as Iranian leaders emphasized the Republican losses.
Today’s statement from the IRGC Navy claimed that four unidentified tankers had struck mines while attempting transits through the southern channel near the coast of Oman. It said that two of the tankers were still ablaze. At the same time, they said two other tankers had been turned back before attempting to make the illegal passage and that they had downed a U.S. MQ-9 drone, marking the 56th of its kind Iran claims to have downed since the start of the war.
Yesterday, the IRGC Navy made a similar unsubstantiated claim, saying that three oil tankers exploded and caught fire after entering an unauthorized route through the Strait of Hormuz and striking sea mines. This came after its so-called Persian Gulf Strait Authority doubled the number of vessels on its non-compliant list.
No independent verification has emerged for most of the claims, although tankers have been known of late to be delaying or not reporting incidents. CENTCOM and the Trump administration have also remained silent, although it has repeated in recent days the assertions that the shipping channels in the Strait of Hormuz have been cleared of mines.
UK Maritime Trade Operations said it received details of only one attack late on Tuesday, November 3. It said a tanker reported being struck by two unknown projectiles into the engine room approximately 14 NM northeast of Lima, Oman. Vanguard Tech is identifying the vessel as the Barbados-registered shadow fleet tanker Grit (298,555 dwt). Built in 2003, it appears to be under Chinese ownership since June 2026.
Grit was one of the vessels Iran placed in the latest round on its non-compliant list. Some reports say the tanker had loaded in Qatar, while TankerTrackers.com posted that the vessel “recently transported Iraqi crude oil to the Gulf of Oman.” The tanker’s AIS signal had been turned off for more than a month.
Lloyd’s List Intelligence also reported one other strike on a bulker early on November 2. It reports the Panama-flagged bulker Era S. (46,681 dwt) was attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz. The vessel was built in 1999 and is managed by Turkish interests.
The claims of strikes came as Iran cited the results of the U.S. midterm elections and said it was evidence the American people did not support the war. Some within Iran repeated the statements of determination to pursue the war, while others called for ending the conflict through dialogue. Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, posted on social media that Americans had said no to war.
Iranian officials continue to insist they gave negotiators seven points that the U.S. must meet before reopening the Strait of Hormuz and that it is the U.S. that did not respond. At the same time, Ahmad Hayat Moghaddam of the Iranian Parliament told the media that they had decided to grant exemptions for transits without limitations to vessels from China, India, Iraq, and Qatar. He noted Iran’s business relations with these four countries.
Get the latest maritime news delivered to your inbox daily.
TankerTrackers.com, however, notes the tanker struck yesterday, Grit , has been transporting Iraqi oil. It also highlighted that roughly 30 percent of the cargo aboard the tankers listed by the PGSA is Iraqi. TankerTrackers.com wrote that “Iraq is not immune to the IRGC.”
Donald Trump, for his part, told reporters that the vote did not reflect views of himself, as he was not on the ballot. He said Americans might have been reacting to the high gas prices, but reiterated his determination to see the war effort through and ensure Iran never has a nuclear bomb.

articles.title_orig: Joint List says it will back Eisenkot to form Israel’s next government
articles.title_zh: Joint List says it will back Eisenkot to form Israel’s next government
articles.content_orig:
The Joint List alliance of Arab-led parties says it will back Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a new government after last week’s election.
“The Joint List announced today, Thursday, that it will inform the President of the State, Isaac Herzog, this evening of its decision to recommend that Gadi Eisenkot be tasked with forming the government,” the alliance said in a statement.
Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats in Israel’s 120-seat parliament in last week’s general election, a result that could give them significant influence over the formation of the next government.
Once the Joint List’s 11 lawmakers formally submit their recommendation, Eisenkot is expected to have the backing of 67 lawmakers, exceeding the 61-seat majority threshold in the Knesset.
Earlier, Ra’am, an Arab-led party with eight seats, said it would also recommend Eisenkot.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc with 53 seats may not yield 53 endorsements, as Degel HaTorah, which holds four of United Torah Judaism’s seven seats, said it would recommend neither candidate.
The ultra-Orthodox faction broke with Netanyahu over his coalition’s failure to pass legislation exempting Haredi men from military service, The Times of Israel reported.
Netanyahu has also claimed repeatedly and without evidence that Arab parties committed fraud during the elections with foreign backing.
The prime minister and his Likud party have cited a handful of cases, including the arrests of three political activists who allegedly bribed voters before polls opened. They are suspected of connections with the Ra’am party, although the party denies any involvement.
Netanyahu and Likud also suggested that the opposition bloc joining with Arab-led parties would be treasonous. In a statement after the vote, Likud warned that Zionist parties cooperating with the Arab bloc would be “dangerous to Israel”.
Israel’s Central Elections Committee certified the results of the election on Wednesday after finding no evidence of fraud.
President Herzog has also accepted the results and begun consultations with party leaders on whom to task with forming the next government.
He also backed investigating suspected interference but warned against smearing voters who are Palestinian citizens of Israel, saying he had “great respect” for the country’s Palestinian minority, which makes up about 20 percent of the population.
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” he said.
On Wednesday, the president said he had met representatives of the Religious Zionism and Zehut, Shas and Yisrael Beytenu factions.
In a post on X, Herzog said he “received their recommendations regarding the identity of the Knesset member upon whom the task of forming the government should be assigned”.
Herzog added that talks would also continue on Thursday.
Once the consultations end, Herzog will choose the candidate he considers best placed to assemble a coalition, almost certainly Netanyahu or Eisenkot. He has several days to announce his decision, after which the nominee will have 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension.
If neither man succeeds, Israel would hold another election early next year.
Reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh said that if Eisenkot is able to form a government, then he will become Israel’s next prime minister and Netanyahu will likely be the head of the opposition.
“It is up to Gadi Eisenkot to do what he promised, to oust Benjamin Netanyahu. And to do that, he needs to have 61 votes in the Knesset, which means that he needs the votes of the Palestinian-Israeli parties, parties that he does not want to partner up with,” she said.
“But he will most likely have to reach some sort of deal, for [the Palestinian-Israeli parties] to abstain at the very least, to make sure that his government is sworn in and a new chapter in Israeli politics is able to begin,” she added.

articles.title_orig: Micron stock declines 12% as chip sell-off deepens
articles.title_zh: Micron stock declines 12% as chip sell-off deepens
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
You don't have to look that far to grasp the severity of the increasingly painful chip stock sell-off .
Just start with the two names that were (keyword: were) the leaders of the AI-fueled momentum for much of 2026: Sandisk ( SNDK ) and Micron ( MU ).
Micron stock crashed 14% on Thursday, bringing its one-month plunge to a startling 36%.
The rout has brought Micron's forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio down an almost laughable 4.8 times, according to Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace data. Keep in mind Micron is coming off a quarter of strong demand amid memory chip shortages driving up prices.
The Street still expects Micron to grow earnings by at least 17% in its next fiscal year.
Sandisk is in the same valuation boat as Micron, trading at about 4.9 times estimated forward earnings on a P/E basis. Similar to Sandisk, its business has been very strong, and the Street remains bullish on its profit outlook.
Sandisk stock is down 19% today, bringing its one-month drop to 29%.
For perspective here, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) trades at about 18.5 times estimated forward earnings.
The bottom line appears to be this: The market couldn't care less about the valuations on either former AI momentum darling. The prevailing view is that, with Democrats taking control of the House and Senate and victories in key governor races, the construction of new data centers will be slowed.
That could mean fewer orders for Micron and Sandisk and a reassessment of their longer-term earnings power.
In other words, each is likely a value trap — until the dust settles on the AI trade.

articles.title_orig: ‘I worry people will forget Hong Kong’: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
articles.title_zh: ‘I worry people will forget Hong Kong’: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
articles.content_orig:
Wong, 30, in prison since 2020, is only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under national security law
Exclusive: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
The Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has been sentenced to 10 years in prison after earlier pleading guilty to “foreign collusion”, his second conviction under a national security law critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.
Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s 2014 pro-democracy demonstrations, submitted his guilty plea in September. He had been accused of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
In his ruling on Thursday, the high ​court judge William Tam ‌described Wong’s actions as “grave in nature”.
He said Wong had visited the US to seek foreign interference before the national security law’s introduction in 2020, and continued to share posts on social media by Law calling for sanctions after it was enacted.
Wong’s role was to “supply his underground support” and “arouse the attention of foreign countries to bolster the cause”, the judge said. He described Wong’s actions as part of a “scheme” to collude with foreign governments.
Tam said Wong’s sentence would run concurrently with the remaining term of his previous national security offence.
After the ruling, Law said in a statement: “It’s incredibly sad to see my friend Joshua Wong suffer another sentencing over his peaceful advocacy work for Hong Kong’s democracy. The signal the sentencing sent to the world is that [China] is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil.”
Amnesty International’s deputy regional director, Sarah Brooks, said: “Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s national security law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security.”
Wong wore a dark blue shirt and thick rimmed spectacles in court, and nodded and bowed as supporters waved. Dozens of people had waited in line outside the court building for the hearing, amid a heavy police presence. A group of international diplomats was also present for the sentencing.
The former student leader is already serving a prison term of four years and eight months, imposed in November 2024, for conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.
The US consulate in Hong Kong said in a statement that it “strongly condemns” the additional sentence and called for Wong’s immediate release. “Wong has been unjustly imprisoned since December 2020, demonstrating that Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong,” a consular spokesperson said.
Shortly afterwards, China warned against “irresponsible” remarks on Hong Kong’s judicial affairs. “Relevant parties should earnestly respect China’s sovereignty, respect Hong Kong’s legal system, stop making irresponsible remarks regarding the trial of … judicial cases,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told reporters.
Wong, 30, gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests , which paralysed the city’s financial centre and galvanised a generation of young people. In October 2014, he appeared on the cover of Time magazine under the headline: “The face of protest.”
When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the protests and immediately took to the streets.
The following year, Beijing introduced a sweeping national security law it said was needed to restore stability to the former British colony, but critics say has been used to target political opposition, dissolve civil society groups and silence independent media.
Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law.

articles.title_orig: After Riots and Protests, French Workers Are Going on Strike
articles.title_zh: After Riots and Protests, French Workers Are Going on Strike
articles.content_orig:
• General strike : French riot police have fired tear gas in Paris and Lyon while scuffles have broken out in Nantes and authorities have arrested agitators who vandalized a Rennes hotel. But overall, the roughly 200 demonstrations across France on Thursday – attended by almost 600,000 people – have remained relatively peaceful.
• Widespread disruptions : The strike is organized by L’intersyndicale, the group that represents all of France’s main trade unions. Education, health care, public transportation and other sectors have been impacted with many services closed for the day.
• Europe discontent : Anti-government protests have swept across the continent in recent weeks. In Greece , students and teachers gathered in central Athens on Thursday to stress the importance of free public education and protest the rising housing and food costs affecting students.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will hold a “social conference” with employers and unions next Monday as hundreds of thousands of people participate in protests across the country.
The conference will be aimed at addressing questions around “purchasing power and wages,” the prime minister’s office said in a statement .
Today’s general strike and protests have been organized by L’intersyndicale, the group that represents all of France’s main trade unions.
Place de la Nation, in eastern Paris, is a historic plaza synonymous with protest. Marches often end here, and we’re used to seeing huge clouds of tear gas as protesters clash with police.
But tonight, it’s quite an unusual and arresting sight to see the square so full after dark. A huge mass of people continue to stand still beneath a monument celebrating the triumph of the French Republic.
The protest in Paris was authorized by city officials to wrap up at 7 p.m. local time (1 p.m. ET). But with less than 30 minutes to go, it’s unlikely everyone will be able to disperse quickly.
Although this movement initially began with students protesting the state of the education system, it has morphed into one that includes several other concerns united by a key factor: the poor state of the economy.
Protesters on Thursday said they are anxious about low salaries, which have not kept up with inflation, as well as underresourced public services.
“There is a lot of concern about the future, notably the issues of salaries, public services,” Alice Martinovic, an 18-year-old student participating in the Paris protest, told Reuters.
“I hope in the upcoming elections the candidates will really think about this movement and include the opinions of young people, of students, who are now joined by a lot of other workers.”
Meanwhile, Mehdi Dumontroty, a 45-year-old firefighter also protesting in Paris, told Reuters that “our pay has not kept up with inflation.”
“What happened this summer proves that we were right when we said we needed more resources to deal with the crisis that we faced,” he said, referencing fierce wildfires which swept across southern France amid record-breaking, climate change-fueled heat waves.
Almost 600,000 protesters are on the streets of France today, the country’s interior ministry has just estimated, making Thursday the biggest day of protests since this current wave of unrest began in September.
Earlier today, at 1 p.m. local time (7 a.m. ET), the ministry had estimated that 270,000 people were protesting but that number excluded Paris, where a march began this afternoon.
The ministry is expected to release its final figures later today but, as of now, its current estimates indicate that these demonstrations are not quite as big as the 2023 pension reform protests.
French education minister Édouard Geffray has condemned what he said was a “deliberate act of arson” at a school near the city of Toulouse in southern France.
The minister thanked firefighters and law enforcement officials for helping to “limit the damage” cause by the flames.
“This deliberate act of arson could have had tragic consequences for human life. I condemn it in the strongest possible terms and call on everyone to condemn it unequivocally,” he added, while vowing to hold those responsible to account.
Earlier, France’s interior ministry said the blaze started after fireworks were directed at an office hosting the school’s student services.
Authorities in Rennes said they arrested “several dozen” masked individuals who vandalized a hotel, threw objects at police and “violently attacked” union members who were protesting earlier today.
Photos taken by local media show that vandals smashed the hotel’s glass doors and painted graffiti on windows.
Some masked individuals also tried to erect barricades to block some of the city’s roads, lit fires in garbage bins, and threw heavy pétanque balls – used in a popular French game – at police, authorities added.
Despite violent clashes like this, however, the protests today have largely been peaceful even as they have been attended by hundreds of thousands of people.
As today’s march in Paris got underway, the trade unions were in a jubilant mood. Music blared out as the crowd, dominated by left-wing groups, sang and chanted slogans against the government and the far-right.
A police helicopter buzzed above, but in the confines of the avenue we were walking down, there was little sense of the heavy police presence around the protest.
In the distance, the soaring statue of Marianne – the national symbol of France – got smaller and smaller as the march inched its way forward.
The protest route is packed. The movement of the crowd has been brought to a near standstill at points by the sheer quantity of people.
Later, several protesters were seen lying on the ground being treated by street medics, with blood flowing from the head of an older man. A bystander said the man was struck by police, but an officer at the scene said they were unaware of any incident.
At one point, protesters scattered as tear gas was deployed by police, followed by mass cries of “everyone hates the police.”
The mood of the crowd has lost its upbeat feel.
Several of France’s biggest unions, representing everyone from students, teachers and postal workers to doctors, pharmacists and transport workers, have called for a nationwide strike. So, how is that affecting these essential services?
Schools: About 13% of all school staff are participating in the strikes, France’s education ministry estimates, including 16% of all teachers. Around 19% of schools and 18% of colleges across France are affected by the strike.
Universities: About one in three of France’s higher education are “disrupted” because of the strikes and protests, the government told CNN.
Hospitals: Very few public hospital staff – only about 4% of the workforce – are participating in the strike, France’s healthcare ministry told CNN. “No significant disruption to healthcare services has been reported,” the ministry added. Two of France’s main unions representing both public and private healthcare workers had called on them to strike, citing the high cost of living and the deterioriation of public services.
Transport: Four in 10 of today’s scheduled trains have been canceled, though a handful of those cancelations are due to other factors like unavailable equipment, according to tracking website Trayn.
The labor unions that have called today’s demonstrations in France are demanding higher wages and pensions. In particular, the largest of the unions – the CGT – says the minimum wage needs to be increased immediately by 10%.
Last month, the CGT claimed there had been a big increase in the number of professions paying some employees less than the minimum wage. Another union - the CFDT – is demanding a 100 euro increase in the minimum monthly wage, about 7%.
Maud Millier, a CGT official in Lyon, said that the government’s announced minimum wage increase, from November 1, amounts to just €15 for someone earning the minimum wage, which she said was nowhere near enough given rising fuel and food pr

articles.title_orig: China Resources Longdation's Aethereal Cybersecurity and GCSA Jointly Establish the Centre for AI and Cybersecurity Research
articles.title_zh: China Resources Longdation's Aethereal Cybersecurity and GCSA Jointly Establish the Centre for AI and Cybersecurity Research
articles.content_orig:
HONG KONG , Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- China Resources Longdation's Aethereal Cybersecurity and Global Cybersecurity Alliance Limited (GCSA) have announced the joint establishment of the Centre for AI and Cybersecurity Research. The initiative brings together both parties' technological expertise and industry resources in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and industrial applications to advance research, product innovation, and industry collaboration.
Founded in 1982, China Resources Longdation operates across property management, asset management, and community services. Its Aethereal Cybersecurity business specializes in AI-driven digital transformation and cybersecurity services for government agencies and enterprises, providing professional technologies and solutions to Hong Kong SAR 's government departments, public institutions, and businesses, supported by relevant cybersecurity qualifications. GCSA is committed to advancing technological innovation, research collaboration, and international exchange in cybersecurity, with a particular focus on emerging security challenges involving AI, Web3, and digital finance.
The two parties will strengthen their cooperation in cybersecurity. The Centre will focus on joint research and development in AI-powered fraud prevention, cyber threat detection, digital financial security, and cybersecurity automation. Key areas of exploration include AI deception honeypots, intelligent fraud detection, threat intelligence analysis, and security platforms, with an emphasis on practical applications.
By combining their respective resources and professional service capabilities, the partnership aims to foster cross-organizational collaboration in AI and cybersecurity, contributing to the development of the digital economy and cybersecurity industry.
Contact: Laber Mann, media@gcsa.com

articles.title_orig: Shield AI To Hit $28.8 Billion Value With $5.3 Billion Radar Acquisition
articles.title_zh: Shield AI To Hit $28.8 Billion Value With $5.3 Billion Radar Acquisition
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — Defense tech firm Shield AI is acquiring Echodyne , a provider of counter-drone radar systems, in a $5.3 billion deal, the companies announced today.
The deal, which is expected to close in early 2027, will give Shield an in-house counter-UAS offering, according to a company statement. Echodyne says its counter-drone systems are “used by defense, government and commercial customers in more than 40 countries.” Further, its Metamaterials Electronically Scanned Array (MESA) system was selected in September by the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401 to supply counter-drone systems to the US military.
The addition of a counter-drone radar system is an interesting add to Shield, which has several different product lines, ranging from autonomy software that has been used on multiple Pentagon projects, to the large X-Bat drone the company now hopes to market globally .
Shield has a history of product expansion through acquisition. It’s V-Bat drone, and hence the push for X-Bat, came form a 2021 acquisition of Martin UAV. And earlier this year, the firm closed on the purchase of Aechelon Technologies, a simulation software firm.
“The acquisition of Echodyne dramatically accelerates our efforts to meet growing customer demand for multi-mission capabilities, provides increased access to a rapidly expanding counter-drone industry, and further diversifies our revenue streams with sustained, compelling growth for the combined company,” Shield CEO Gary Steele said in a statement, noting the company structure now consists of three buckets: autonomy software, autonomous systems and mission systems.
“Hundreds of customers rely on our radars to detect and track drones, protect people and infrastructure, secure borders, and ensure safe airspace operations. Shield shares our view that autonomous systems can only act on what they can sense, and superior sensors lead to superior systems and outcomes,” Echodyne CEO Eben Frankenberg added. “By joining Shield, we’re creating a company with the size and breadth to deliver even more value to our broad range of defense, government, and commercial customers around the globe.”
Echodyne will operate as a business unit within Shield’s mission systems business, with Frankenberg staying on and reporting up to Steele as part of the company’s executive team. There are no planned workforce reductions, and Echodyne employees will not be required to relocate, according to a Shield spokesperson. Longer term, there will likely be greater integration of Echodyne products across Shield’s portfolio.
A commitment to long-term operational value.
While the company is not announcing any “specific aircraft integrations” right now, the spokesperson noted that “Autonomous systems can only act on what they can sense, and Shield expects autonomous aircraft to need more capable onboard sensors in the coming years. Echodyne’s radar is built for that use. The acquisition also adds radar engineering, manufacturing capacity and a commercial customer base to Shield’s business.”
The spokesperson added that the Echodyne deal has no impact on the recent decision to work with RTX for a radar on X-Bat, saying that work “is separate from this acquisition.”
Of the $5.3 billion deal, $4.8 billion will be paid out at closing with another $500 million paid out upon Echodyne meeting spelled out performance targets. Coinciding with the deal, Shield raised $2.5 billion through Series H funding and investments from Blackstone and JPMorgan Chase.
The spokesperson also noted that the company “will continue to look at acquisitions as part of its growth strategy.”

articles.title_orig: Marc Lore's Wonder confidentially files for IPO
articles.title_zh: Marc Lore's Wonder confidentially files for IPO
articles.content_orig:
Food startup Wonder has confidentially filed for an initial public offering, the company said Thursday.
Created by serial entrepreneur Marc Lore in 2018, Wonder advertises itself as "the best restaurants from across the country, all in one place," available for delivery and takeout on its vertically integrated app.
Originally envisioned as a new take on food delivery through sprinter vans outfitted with mobile kitchens, Wonder has grown to roughly 170 brick-and-mortar locations throughout the U.S. Its locations serve menu items from more than two dozen "restaurants" across a variety of cuisines, some with branding from celebrity chefs.
Starting Nov. 17, the company plans to introduce more dining options through Wonder Create. Influencers, entrepreneurs and brands can pay $10 a month to start their own restaurant business based out of a Wonder location and earn a portion of the revenue from orders.
Wonder has spent at least $1 billion on acquisitions, such as delivery service Grubhub, meal kit brand Blue Apron and delivery and logistics provider Relay, along with some buzzy restaurant concepts. Wonder has been able to afford such expensive dealmaking thanks to more than $3 billion in venture funding.
Wonder's Series D fundraising round earlier this year raised its pre-money valuation to $9 billion.
With the proceeds from an IPO, Wonder will be able to make more acquisitions and work toward its goal of making food more accessible, Lore told CNBC in September.
But as a public company, Wonder will also likely face investor scrutiny. Weak consumer sentiment has weighed on restaurant stocks recently, plus market volatility has resulted in a shaky IPO market for companies across a range of industries.
Lore previously founded Diapers.com and Jet.com, which he sold to Amazon and Walmart, respectively.

articles.title_orig: Clashes erupt in France as ‘Black Thursday’ protests sweep the nation
articles.title_zh: Clashes erupt in France as ‘Black Thursday’ protests sweep the nation
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — Riot police clashed with protesters in Lyon on Thursday as a nationwide public sector strike tapped into growing anger over deteriorating services and the rising cost of living.
Paris’ iconic Eiffel Tower was closed because of the strike.
Officers clad in black helmets and protective clothing charged at crowds in Lyon after the demonstrations against rising living costs and in support of the high school protest movement turned violent and fires were set in the streets. Water cannons were also deployed. Some of the protesters wore gas masks and safety glasses as a precaution against tear gas.
Images from Paris showed students and other protesters facing off against riot police.
Police were “keeping the situation under control, but it remains tense,” the French Interior Ministry said in a statement at 1 p.m. local time (7 a.m. ET).
“Several violent acts have been committed as part of the high school student movement,” the statement said. After fireworks were fired at a school near the southern city of Toulouse, a fire broke out “that burned the student services office,” it added.
In the city of Rennes in northwest France, metal pétanque balls were thrown at officers, the statement said, adding that police had been pelted with other projectiles in the cities of Pau and Orleans.
Around 250 rallies against rising living costs had been planned in cities and towns across the country and hundreds of thousands of people would likely turn out, unions said before the events kicked off.
France’s main unions, including the CGT and CNT representing public and private sector workers, and the UNEF, representing students, warned the government of President Emmanuel Macron’s that the country was on the brink or recession.
“Everything is going up except wages and pensions,” they said in a joint statement. “Anger is immense.”
“The situation in this country is fragile. The pressing social and environmental challenges must be addressed without delay,” the statement added.
The movement grew from a student protest over staff shortages at the Antoine de Saint-Exupéry High School in Créteil, a southeastern suburb of Paris. Videos of the blockade spread on social media, and soon protests expanded to high schools across the nation.
As the movement grew, the list of grievances expanded beyond the failings of the public school system to encompass broader economic, political and social dissatisfaction. Soon, university students, teachers, parents and politicians also joined.
Hundreds of thousands of protesters have since taken to the streets as the demonstrations expanded, with participants holding signs criticizing the far-right National Rally party and warning of the risks of climate change and artificial intelligence. A multitude of Palestinian flags have also been seen.
Macron, who will leave office in May, convened a defense ‌and security meeting Wednesday ahead of the protests. Later, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that 70,000 police officers would be deployed Thursday, backed by armored vehicles, drones and helicopters.
Police have previously been criticized for injuring protesters with heavy-handed tactics. Last month, a 15-year-old was maimed by a sting ball grenade fired by police and a 14-year-old suffered a jaw fracture in a similar incident.
Several other have also suffered life-changing injuries and a 59-year-old man, identified as Christophe M, died Oct. 17 of “a critical cardio-respiratory failing” after leaving Paris’ Place de la République which had been tear-gassed be police. An investigation into his death is ongoing.
Zacharie Petit reported from Paris and Henry Austin from London.
Zacharie Petit is a producer in Paris.
Henry Austin is a senior editor for NBC News Digital based in London.

articles.title_orig: Bad News for Italian Chef Who Balked at Pineapple Pizza
articles.title_zh: Bad News for Italian Chef Who Balked at Pineapple Pizza
articles.content_orig:
An Italian chef sacked from a Brisbane restaurant had refused to put pineapple on a pizza because it was an "insult to his culture".
Davide Tamburella was fired from the now-closed La Costa restaurant in May, a fortnight after a meeting with management who had a string of complaints about the chef's behaviour.
Among them were Tamburella's refusal to provide ham and pineapple pizza for guests at a function. At the time, the chef had stated that any direction from management "need not be followed when it is offensive to his culture".
The details came to light after the chef went to Australia's Fair Work Commission claiming he had been unfairly dismissed.
In its ruling released on Tuesday, the commission noted that Tamburella's refusal to put pineapple on the pizzas was because "he considers, as an Italian, that putting pineapple on a pizza is an insult to his culture".
It also noted that it was the third time Tamburella had refused to use the fruit on pizzas in the past four years.
He had previously requested his boss to "check how important it is for Italians not to put pineapple on a pizza".
The state of Queensland, where the restaurant is located, is considered Australia's pineapple heartland and produces all of the country's commercially-grown pineapples.
On the Sunshine Coast, visitors regularly stop to take photos next to The Big Pineapple, a heritage-listed 16m-tall fibreglass model of the fruit, which has become a local landmark.
Other concerns were raised about Tamburella using foul language, his communication style and "escalation of frustration in the workplace".
The ruling also detailed an incident at work in April this year where Tamburella fractured bones in his right hand when he struck a metal hand rail.
Tamburella had been hoping the restaurant would sponsor a visa for him that allows skilled workers to be permanent residents.
However after his sacking, the restaurant ended that  process, the tribunal heard.
He lost his unfair dismissal claim on the grounds that the application had been filed too late, according to the ruling.
The restaurant's managing director, Elliot Ingram, told the Daily Mail there was "more to this story than a pizza topping".
The BBC has approached Tamburella for comment.
On the chef's LinkedIn profile, he describes himself as someone who, throughout his career, has focused on "delivering exceptional food" and "improving business performance".
Three months ago he posted a "letter for chefs" with the theme "respecting the ingredients".
The LinkedIn profile states he now works at another Brisbane restaurant. A BBC check has found that pineapple is not on its menu.

articles.title_orig: Record share of first-time homebuyers paying in cash as Great Wealth Transfer picks up steam
articles.title_zh: Record share of first-time homebuyers paying in cash as Great Wealth Transfer picks up steam
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The Great Wealth Transfer is starting to impact the housing market.
A record share of first-time homebuyers are paying for their properties in cash, a sign that more buyers are likely using money they inherited from older generations to help fund their purchases.
Last year, 1 in 10 first-time buyers did an all-cash transaction, according to a new report from the National Association of Realtors, the fourth straight year with an increase, and the largest share since the trade group began collecting data on those transactions in 2003. Among first-time all-cash buyers, 28% reported using an inheritance to help fund their deal, compared with just 9% of first-time buyers who financed.
As home prices hover near all-time highs and mortgage rates stay north of 7% , pricing out many prospective buyers, some portion of those buyers may simply be waiting for an inheritance or other significant help from wealthy baby boomers or members of the Silent Generation.
"It is critical when analyzing first-time buyers to understand there is a growing divide among those who are saving independently and priced out of homeownership, versus those who are waiting on the sidelines but then given a generational transfer of wealth," the report said.
Buyers reliant on wealth transfers look different from those who finance and use their own savings. As modern life expectancy increases, delaying inheritances, first-time all-cash buyers are typically deep into middle age. The median first-time buyer paying all cash is 54 years old, according to the report, significantly older than the median age of 38 for first-time buyers financing their homes.
Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.

articles.title_orig: Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger found dead in Berlin hotel
articles.title_zh: Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger found dead in Berlin hotel
articles.content_orig:
Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger was found dead in a hotel in Berlin on Wednesday, the German capital's public prosecutor's office said.
Aiwanger was Bavaria's deputy premier, economy minister and the chairman of the right-wing populist Free Voters party. He was 55 years old.
The circumstances surrounding Aiwanger's death are still unclear. Police and prosecutors in the German capital have launched an investigation.
On Wednesday evening, investigators said the goal is to "determine the specific cause of death and the circumstances surrounding it, as well as to rule out any possible foul play."
Aiwanger had been feeling unwell on Wednesday, German tabloid Bild reported.
He was scheduled to deliver a speech at the opening of a party office in Berlin but canceled his appearance for health reasons, German news agency dpa reported.
Aiwanger's body was found on Wednesday evening at the "Neuer Fritz" Hotel on Friedrichstrasse in Berlin-Mitte, according to Bild .
Bavarian state premier, the Christian Social Union 's Markus Söder, has said he is "deeply shocked" by the news of his deputy's death.
"The sudden death of Hubert Aiwanger is an absolute tragedy," Söder said in a post on X.
"Our thoughts are now first and foremost with his family and his children. We mourn with them and pray for them."
Born in Lower Bavaria in southern Germany , Aiwanger was elected to the Bavarian State Parliament in 2008 with the Free Voters and became their parliamentary group leader.
Since 2018, his party has been in a coalition with the center-right CSU, the Bavarian sister party of the ruling Christian Democratic Union (CDU) . Aiwanger served as the state's Minister of Economic Affairs and deputy premier.
Aiwanger was the face of the Free Voters in Bavaria and across Germany, and was known for his combative approach.
But his political success in the state did not translate to the national level, as the Free Voters never won enough seats to enter the Bundestag , Germany's federal parliament.
In the weeks before state elections in 2023, Aiwanger became embroiled in a national scandal when the Süddeutsche Zeitung reported that he had written an antisemitic leaflet during high school in the 1980s, which included references to Nazi-era atrocities such as Auschwitz.
He is survived by two children. He was not married but lived with Tanja Schweiger, a district administrator for the Free Voters.
