Captain Carter Brown, an Alaskan fishing guide, shares his experience after a grizzly bear swam directly up to his boat in Soldotna, Alaska, on ‘The Story.’
A Canadian woman and her daughter were killed in a suspected grizzly bear attack over the weekend while hiking on a trail near their home, according to authorities.
Jennifer Balcarras, 48, an art therapist, and her daughter, Selah Reed, 20, went missing Saturday after going for a walk on the Snooka West Trail, just minutes from their home in Bella Coola, British Columbia .
Loved ones grew concerned when Balcarras failed to show up for a scheduled online meet-up on Saturday, her brother, Matt Balcarras, told The Vancouver Sun .
Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her 20-year-old daughter, Selah Reed, were killed in a suspected grizzly bear attack. (Facebook/Josh Kara Balcarras)
A PRACTICAL GUIDE TO NOT GETTING MAULED BY A BEAR WHILE HIKING OR CAMPING THIS SUMMER
After failing to reach the pair, relatives asked the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) for a welfare check on Sunday morning.
Authorities discovered Balcarras' vehicle parked at the trailhead . Her body was recovered Monday, and search teams found Reed's body on Tuesday.
A Grizzly bear in Jasper National Park, Canada. A Canadian woman and her daughter were killed in a suspected bear attack in British Columbia over the weekend, conservation officials said. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)
GRIZZLY BEAR MAULS HIKER, DRAGS HIM DOZENS OF FEET ON GLACIER NATIONAL PARK TRAIL
"There was evidence to suggest a bear may have been involved," Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service, said in a video update posted to social media.
Tyre noted that officers were actively working to "locate and capture any bears involved" and said it was not immediately clear if more than one animal was responsible.

"Any captured bear will be assessed," conservation officials added in a statement. "If it is determined to have been involved in the attack, it will be dispatched in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety."
Matt Balcarras expressed shock over the location of the attack, emphasizing that his sister and niece were experienced in the region.
"They were not naive city folks," he said. "They were strong women living the life."

The tragic encounter came less than a year after a grizzly bear injured 11 people , including fourth- and fifth-grade students, during a school field trip near Bella Coola.

articles.title_orig: AI backlash threatens trillion-dollar data centre boom, say tech leaders
articles.title_zh: AI backlash threatens trillion-dollar data centre boom, say tech leaders
articles.content_orig:
A stunning upset in the Texas governor race and sweeping Democratic victories across the country threaten to curtail the biggest-ever spending boom in US history.
That could disrupt a key growth engine for America’s economy .
Come January, states controlled by Democrats who support expanding or extending AI construction moratoriums will account for 45% of America’s planned data center capacity, according to Goldman Sachs. A quarter of America’s planned AI infrastructure buildout is set to take place in Texas alone.
That doesn’t mean half of America’s planned data centers are on hold. Demand for AI is off the charts. Donald Trump is still president, and he’s already waving around his veto hat. And Democratic governors couldn’t stop every data center from being constructed even if they wanted to.
But Tuesday’s election nevertheless represents a paradigm shift that could alter the pace and path of America’s nonstop AI spending spree – an investment boom that has, according to ING economists, accounted for as much as a quarter of total US economic growth this year.
Communities fighting against the buildings that power AI
Those economic benefits are already real, supporting thousands of jobs. And AI has the potential to revolutionize the way we work.
But an AI data center slowdown could come with important silver linings. It could rein in unfettered growth that has contributed to rebounding inflation and led to widespread public antipathy toward the technology and the data centers that house it. It could also curtail some questionable business models that have raised serious skepticism on Wall Street.
Tapping the brakes could ultimately put AI – and the US economy – on a more sustainable path.
AI infrastructure spending is expected to approach $1 trillion a year, every year, for the foreseeable future, according to Columbia Business School economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. As a percentage of America’s gross domestic product, that would outpace every other investment boom in modern US history – including the construction of the railroads.
The outcome of Tuesday’s elections could slow that spending, with vast consequences for the thousands of jobs and massive amounts of economic development that AI supports.
Democrats gained gubernatorial seats in Nevada, Georgia, Ohio and Texas, where candidates campaigned on tightening data center regulations. Proposals from the governors-elect include ending tax breaks, tightening climate and electricity restrictions and allowing local governments to impose their own moratoriums on data center construction.
But Texas is the big kahuna. Wells Fargo estimates that for every 10% reduction in planned Texas data center capacity, Big Tech companies will reduce their AI infrastructure spending by a stunning 1.6% (a lot of money when you’re measuring spending in the trillions of dollars).
State and local politicians have a lot of jurisdiction and sway over that spending: enough to change whether some projects get financed, said Mona Dajani, co-chair of Cooley’s infrastructure, energy and real estate practice.
Hundreds of data center developments that are still awaiting permits, utility service or tax incentives could be particularly exposed, Dajani noted. But even active construction projects could be threatened. Texas law grandfathers in some projects’ permits, protecting them from future changes to local permitting requirements – but that doesn’t resolve state permitting changes or electrical service guarantees that Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa could vacate.
The wait for approvals could add significant costs for AI companies, Dajani said: Interest, equipment commitments and utility expenses will all continue to accrue, even while a project is on ice. At some point, existing projects could stop being financially viable.
If that happens, AI companies – who have already strained to build out data centers fast enough to meet their anticipated demand – may not be able to meet their explosive spending targets.
“This is a rare case where state and local leaders have influence of geopolitical-level import,” said Harry Krejsa, director of studies at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology.
Data centers aren’t exclusively a Democratic issue: Americans have displayed bipartisan consensus for putting guardrails around data center buildouts.
Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott had already imposed a data center moratorium that Hinojosa campaigned on extending until lawmakers establish stronger AI regulations.
But Trump had railed against any attempts to stymie AI’s growth and spending, citing economic and national security – particularly in the high-stakes race against China. Many Republican politicians who may have otherwise supported AI regulations, including frameworks for data center construction, remained silent.
Still, there’s evidence that the AI buildout could be on an unsustainable path.
The United States had 5,427 data centers at the end of last year, according to Stanford University’s AI Index Report , and AI companies have announced plans for 3,969 new US data centers, according to Aterio , a data center research company. But only about 800 are under construction, and AI experts have raised doubts about the viability of many of the announced projects.
If Tuesday’s election results trigger an investment slowdown, that could trim some of the industry’s fat.
Example A: CoreWeave, a neocloud business that rents out computing capacity, recently projected such extensive losses that its bond yields surged to 15% – the danger zone. That was particularly troubling, because its expected return on investment was only around 9%.
In other words, CoreWeave loses money on every single dollar it spends on expanding its data center capacity.
Deep-pocketed hyperscalers – Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft – don’t have that problem. But their stocks have been slammed in recent weeks as investors grow impatient with what they view as an unsustainable amount of spending that may not return profits for years.
“AI is catching a break here,” said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM US.
Brusuelas expects growth to slow from last quarter’s 3.4% pace to something closer to 2.4% if there is an AI slowdown. That’s still solid long-term growth. And America’s economy is massive and diverse. Investment that otherwise would have gone to data centers can go elsewhere.
“It’s slowing, but it doesn’t mean we’re going to have a recession,” Brusuelas said.
It also presents an opportunity for AI companies to get smart about their future AI data center rollouts – and get put on a more sustainable course.
The helter-skelter approach to data center construction has resulted in significant amounts of money getting flushed down the toilet in unworkable projects – collateral damage from massive competition to be first and biggest. Data centers already face $200 billion in project delays, according to Mike Mathews, global digital infrastructure practice leader at risk adviser Marsh.
A more rational, politically sensitive approach could create longer-term benefits for the communities that host the data centers and for the AI companies themselves.
There’s precedent for that. In the previous decade, the Googles of the world built out data centers for the cloud computing revolution, promoting the fact that they’d be built sustainably with renewable energy – even before it was cost-effective to do that. A similar, community-based approach could provide AI companies with the compute they need and give them the political and social license to operate their data centers for the long haul.
“Like the saying goes: If you want to go fast, you go it alone; if you want to go far you go together,” said Krejsa. “If you squander political license to operate at home, that’ll be a bigger impediment to remaining competitive with China.”

articles.title_orig: YouTube rolling out app redesign without Subscriptions tab, and everyone hates it
articles.title_zh: YouTube rolling out app redesign without Subscriptions tab, and everyone hates it
articles.content_orig:
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.
Google seems to be taking multiple stabs at tweaking how the bottom navigation bar in the YouTube app looks and works. After removing the Subscriptions tab from the navigation bar , the company is now experimenting with a new floating design.
According to a Reddit post by user SameRecognition5543, Google has started testing a floating navigation bar in the YouTube app on Android. The design looks heavily inspired by the Liquid Glass aesthetic of iOS 27, leading some users to accuse Google of abandoning its own Material 3 Expressive design language in favor of Apple’s Liquid Glass.
Google seems to be running a very limited test for the floating navigation bar on Android. We checked on multiple devices and couldn’t spot the new navigation bar test on any of them. However, we did spot the new floating navigation bar on a couple of iPhones. Google may be prioritizing an iPhone rollout first, which makes sense since iOS introduced the Liquid Glass design language.
Meanwhile, if you like the new look and don’t want to wait for Google to eventually roll it out to your device, there is a workaround you can use. The Morphe YouTube patcher has already been updated with a similar floating navigation bar featuring a Liquid Glass design. First, enable pre-release patches in Morphe on your Android phone. Then, go to Settings > General > Navigation bar and turn on the “Enable glass navigation bar” toggle.
User opinion on the new floating navigation bar is split. Several users are waiting for the update to reach their devices and are using Morphe in the meantime. However, other users aren’t too happy about the iOS-like design. Either way, this might well be the future of YouTube’s navigation bar on Android. If you don’t like it, you can take solace in the fact that Google’s rollouts are infamously slow and phased, so you might not have to see it for a while, even when it does start rolling out.
Read what readers said or add your take.

articles.title_orig: Why Sandisk Stock Keeps Going Down
articles.title_zh: Why Sandisk Stock Keeps Going Down
articles.content_orig:
For investors, it's not as much fun owning Sandisk ( SNDK -19.20% ) as it once was.
Shares of Sandisk, one of the world's leading producers of NAND flash memory for PCs, mobile devices, and -- increasingly -- artificial intelligence data centers , are still up 400% over the past 52 weeks. That's great for investors who got in on the ground floor. More recent Sandisk investors, however, have suffered terribly as Sandisk shares shed 36% of their value over just the last six trading days.
And as of 10 a.m. ET Thursday, Sandisk stock is down another 14.5%.
Image source: Getty Images.
Why is Sandisk stock still going down? Some blame Chinese memory chipmaker CXMT, which has been in the news a lot lately for boasting it invented a new "4F square" memory chip and plans to market it as high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for data centers.
Earlier today, CXMT announced it's received $1 billion in customer prepayments for its DRAM chips through the end of September, "a 15.7-fold increase from ... the end of 2025," according to DigiTimes.
NASDAQ · As of 1:58 PM ET 11/05/26
Should this worry Sandisk investors? Not necessarily.
Firstly, investors need to remember that although both CXMT and Sandisk make computer memory , CXMT focuses on DRAM, while Sandisk produces NAND flash memory exclusively. While competing tangentially in the "memory market," CXMT is not a direct competitor to Sandisk.
One area where the companies may compete in future is if Sandisk's invention of high-bandwidth flash (HBF) memory takes off as an alternative to HBM and CXMT succeeds in producing DRAM chips capable of being used as HBM. As DigiTimes reports, however, CXMT is struggling to transition its DRAM to HBM, and yield rates for its "next-generation HBM3E products" are only 20% to 30%.
If that's the best CXMT can do, Sandisk investors may have even less to worry about .

SpaceX ( SPCX ) and Tesla ( TSLA ) stocks extended declines on Thursday, each dropping roughly 9%. Shares of the Elon Musk-led companies were pounded after Democrats won control of the House and Senate this week, raising concerns over regulatory hurdles for data center buildouts in the US and merger aspirations between the two companies.
The Democratic win in Texas, where both SpaceX and Tesla are headquartered, is at the center of the concern. The state flipped blue at the gubernatorial level and saw the Senate seat won by James Talarico, with whom Musk got into fierce spats on social media leading up to the elections.
"We will believe a SpaceX/Tesla merger happens but now faces a much tougher regulatory roadmap to get this deal done in 2027 given this new political blue roadmap in DC/Texas," Yorkville's partner and managing director Dan Ives wrote on Thursday.
Elon Musk said on SpaceX's third quarter earnings call last month that he thinks merging the company with Tesla ( TSLA ) would be a good idea and revealed that both companies are exploring a potential deal.
Earlier this year, Musk also announced the launch of a Terafab, a massive semiconductor manufacturing complex in Texas that would supply SpaceX and Tesla.
Worries over a slowdown in data center build-outs also dampened shares of Texas-based SpaceX, which has increasingly leaned into AI compute as a revenue source.
Ives said while Big Tech and hyperscaler capex should still easily exceed $1 trillion in 2027, the growth rate into 2028 "will clearly moderate significantly as the data center buildout comes at a much slower pace given the political map, especially in the state of Texas."
On Wednesday, Goldman Sachs analysts also calculated, "Democratic wins at the state and local level are likely to lead to short-term data center moratoria, potentially affecting about 45% of planned US data center capacity expansion.

articles.title_orig: The US Midterm Elections: Views From China - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: The US Midterm Elections: Views From China - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. midterm elections on November 3 were closely watched around the world as a way to gauge public support for the polarizing administration of Donald Trump. The verdict is in: the opposition Democratic Party won big, taking control of both houses of Congress with majorities Democrats haven’t enjoyed in years. Several states elected Democratic senators and governors for the first time in decades – in some cases, nearly a century .
Officially, of course, China won’t comment on the results of the election. That, as Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters on November 4, is “a domestic affair” of the United States. “China stands ready to continue working with the U.S. to uphold and deliver on the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state,” Mao said.
In a speech delivered on election day, Xie Feng, China’s ambassador to the United States, said , “A confident and composed China is committed to the steady, sound, and sustainable development of China-U.S. relations… China’s policy toward the United States remains consistent and stable.”
The first news readouts from Xinhua, China’s state news agency, were also terse, although the points of information they chose to include were telling. In one early article , for example, Xinhua did not mention the historic nature of Democratic Party wins, but instead quoted Trump’s social media post that “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” The short, three-paragraph report also devoted the entire last paragraph to comments from a White House official, who predicted U.S. voters “will suffer from severe buyer’s remorse.”
Xinhua published a much longer analysis on November 4, highlighting four “unexpected” outcomes. This article delved into the massive scale of the Democratic victory, from the size of its new House majority to the flipping of Senate seats in traditionally safe Republican states like Texas, Iowa, Kansas, and South Carolina.
Rather than offering perspectives from Chinese analysts, Xinhua’s article extensively cited U.S. media, including this quote from the Wall Street Journal : “Rarely in American politics has a president traded away so much political support so quickly. The losses that Republicans suffered on Tuesday marked one of the most decisive repudiations of a president in modern history.”
Chinese state media had much less to say about the causes of the Republican defeat – again, Beijing’s official line being that this is an “internal affair” of the United States. However, Xinhua did cite the general thesis by U.S. analysts that economic dissatisfaction amid rising prices was the primary culprit. And those rising prices were exacerbated by the Trump administration’s decision to strike Iran. Xinhua published a whole article covering Vice President J.D. Vance’s post-election verdict that the war on Iran had cost the Republicans control of Congress.
One Xinhua report cited Iran’s Speaker of Parliament Mohammad Ghalibaf, who posted on X : “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.”
“What the Chinese public is most concerned about … is the impact of the U.S. midterm election results on the Iran war and Ukraine war,” Mu Chunshan, an independent political analysts based in Beijing, told The Diplomat via email. “They are less focused on the impact on China-U.S. relations. This is because Trump has consistently shown respect to China.”
If Democrats act to restrain Trump’s military operations in Iran, Mu said, it would be align “with China’s long-standing call for a peaceful resolution of the Iran nuclear issue.” He sees the election results as “conducive to China and other countries pushing for a negotiated resolution of the Iran nuclear issue and Strait [of Hormuz] security issues.”
That said, Chinese analysts are well aware of Congress’ limited control over foreign policy. In an pre-election analysis, South China Morning Post cited Zhao Zhijiang , a research assistant at the Beijing-based independent think tank Anbound, as predicting that “Diplomacy may become even more transactional. U.S. policy towards Russia, Iran, Europe and China could swing rapidly between heavy pressuring and partial bargaining.” In other words, China is bracing for impact as a notoriously mercurial leader feels increased political pressure at home.
Diao Daming, an international relations professor at Renmin University in Beijing, told SCMP Trump might become more “legacy-driven” in his pursuit of foreign policy.  “On the other hand, in areas he believes he can control or achieve results quickly, he may also take some risky actions,” Diao said.
With a Trump-Xi summit looming later this month, China will be one of the first to get a feel for how the midterm defeat impacts Trump’s foreign policy style. China is hosting the APEC Leaders’ Meeting from November 18-19, with Trump expected to attend. Beside yet another summit between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping – the third in 2026 alone – there has been much discussion of other potential sideline meetings, including a possible China-Russia-U.S. trilateral.
China had its own reasons to be skeptical about hosting such a meeting . After the midterm outcomes, which will likely result in increased congressional support for Ukraine, there’s even less reason for Beijing to look positively on the prospects of a Putin-Trump-Xi meeting.
“At the APEC summit, if China, the US and Russia hold a trilateral summit, there is a high probability that the Ukraine war will not be discussed, because the midterm results make it harder for Trump to pressure Ukraine into accepting a ‘land-for-peace’ plan.” Mu said. “For China, discussing this is meaningless. Any peace plan must indeed fully take into account the views of Ukraine and Europe. This should be similar to the views of the new U.S. Congress.”
Also with the APEC summit in mind, Chinese policymakers will want to see if Trump is willing to strike a bargain to secure quick economic gains, given U.S. voter anger over the cost of living. There is also hope that a Democratic Congress would do more to push back on Trump’s use of tariffs – a tool that typically belongs to the legislative branch, not the executive, under the U.S. system of government.
“If the Democrats can restrain Trump’s impulses to China and other countries in the areas of tariffs and trade, that would be better for China-U.S. relations,” Mu said.
But few in China expect a Democratic-majority Congress to look too much different. “Structural contradictions exist in China-U.S. relations, and both the two parties share negative views on China, for example on national security or high-tech competition,” Mu noted. “These will not change in any particular way due to the outcome of the midterms.”
More broadly, Chinese analysts largely took the U.S. election results as evidence for already-held assumptions about a crumbling U.S. political system. Xinhua’s own original reporting , including on-the-street interviews with voters, portrayed a sense of pessimism and despair. Nearly all the quotes were from voters who expressed doubt that anything would change, regardless of who is in power. One sample: “I have no confidence in any politician, and I don’t think they will focus on what is right for us.”
That was a far cry from the palpable sense of optimism emanating from the Democratic Party as the election results rolled in. But it does fit nearly with China’s preferred thesis that the United States is locked into an irreversible decline.
And whatever Beijing may say about the election being the United States’ “domestic affair,” it will not be lost on Chinese leaders that an unpopular war far from home, and its economic consequences, resulted in severe political punishment for the ruling party. That will factor in to China’s ongoing calculations about what the Iran-U.S. war might imply about Americans’ appetite for intervention in a Taiwan crisis.

articles.title_orig: Democrats to probe JPMorgan's relationship with Jeffrey Epstein when they take Senate control
articles.title_zh: Democrats to probe JPMorgan's relationship with Jeffrey Epstein when they take Senate control
articles.content_orig:
Senate Democrats are gearing up to investigate JPMorgan Chase 's banking relationship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein once they take control of Congress early next year.
Democratic staffers on the Senate Finance Committee intend to home in on how high-ranking executives at JPMorgan handled Epstein, a source familiar with the panel's thinking told CNBC on Thursday. The person spoke on condition of anonymity because the probe of the nation's biggest bank has not been announced.
The Finance Committee is likely to be chaired beginning in January by Sen. Ron Wyden , an Oregon Democrat who currently is the panel's ranking member. Wyden has made clear he plans to make full use of the subpoena powers that committee majorities wield.
Democratic staffers aim to focus in particular on decisions about Epstein made by Mary Callahan Erdoes, the CEO of JPMorgan's asset and wealth management division, the source said.
JPMorgan declined to comment. The bank has previously said it regrets any association with Epstein but that it did not assist him in committing crimes.
In a 2023 deposition , Erdoes said she was aware as early as 2006 that Epstein was accused of paying cash to have underage girls brought to his home. Epstein had been a client of the bank since 1998.
Epstein became a registered sex offender after pleading guilty in 2008 in Florida to a state criminal charge of procuring an underage girl for prostitution.
JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon in his own, later deposition in 2023, said Erdoes had authority to cut off Epstein as a client. She did not take that step until 2013.
Epstein, a former friend of President Donald Trump , ex-President Bill Clinton and many other high-profile people, died in a jailhouse suicide in August 2019, weeks after being arrested on federal child sex trafficking charges.
A lawyer for the U.S. Virgin Islands told a federal judge in New York in 2023 that JPMorgan "was a full-service bank for Jeffrey Epstein's sex trafficking," and that it waited until after he killed himself to notify the Treasury Department of $1 billion in suspicious transactions related to trafficking by Epstein.
"This was a CYA [cover your a--] reporting after 16 years of all of the monies flowing in his JPMorgan accounts after he was dead," the lawyer, Mimi Liu, said.
JPMorgan has blamed former investment banking chief Jes Staley for concealing or failing to report criminal activity related to Epstein, with whom he had a close relationship.
Staley, who left JPMorgan in 2013 and later became CEO of Barclays before stepping down in 2021, has denied knowledge of Epstein's crimes.
House Oversight Chair James Comer, R-Ky., after a closed-door interview with Staley in July, said that the former executive had encouraged JPMorgan to keep Epstein as a client.
In mid-2023, JPMorgan agreed to a $290 million settlement with victims of Epstein without admitting wrongdoing. That same year, JPMorgan agreed to pay $75 million to settle a separate lawsuit by the U.S. Virgin Islands alleging that the bank facilitated and benefited from the sex trafficking of young women by Epstein.
In August, Wyden released a report accusing top officials at multiple banks of "looking the other way" as Epstein moved hundreds of millions of dollars to finance a yearslong sex trafficking operation.
"The report exposes how top bankers shielded Epstein from federal scrutiny by delaying the reporting of Epstein's suspicious financial activity to the U.S. government, likely in violation of federal anti-money-laundering laws," Wyden's office said in a statement that month.
"It includes new details about the extent of suspicious activity reported by Deutsche Bank after Epstein's death, new details from bank reports filed about suspicious transfers to Epstein through accounts at Bank of America, and names top officials at JPMorgan Chase and other banks who were responsible for reporting Epstein's shady activities to the government but instead protected Epstein in order to gain access to Leon Black and other billionaires."
Black, former CEO of Apollo Global Management, was revealed to have paid Epstein $158 million for financial advice in the years after his 2008 conviction.
In September, Black sued the House oversight panel, seeking to block subpoenas it had issued him for his testimony and for documents related to its Epstein probe.
On Wednesday, Black sued Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is poised to become chair of the Oversight Committee in the next Congress, alleging Garcia defamed him in statements regarding Epstein. The lawsuit focuses on Garcia's claims in a TV interview that Black "is at the center of Jeffrey Epstein's crimes" and "was one of the last people to actually interact" with Epstein before his death, among others.
The Department of Justice's mountain of files related to Epstein became a major focus in late 2025 and early 2026, after Congress passed a bill ordering the DOJ to make those records public.
Trump's name is referenced thousands of times in the files that have been released.
The president has not been charged with any wrongdoing in connection with Epstein, with whom he fell out in the early 2000s.

articles.title_orig: Wendy's turned down Nelson Peltz's $1.4 billion offer. It's betting instead on thicker bacon and whole-leaf lettuce.
articles.title_zh: Wendy's turned down Nelson Peltz's $1.4 billion offer. It's betting instead on thicker bacon and whole-leaf lettuce.
articles.content_orig:
Wendy's on Thursday said it is rejecting a $1.4 billion takeover offer from a group of investors led by Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management.
The group offered $7.35 per share in cash on Oct. 28 to take the struggling burger chain private . In addition to Trian, it included investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners, plus Flynn Group, one of Wendy's largest franchisees.
In February, Wendy's board formed a committee of independent directors to assess any potential bid from Trian in response to a regulatory filing from the firm. The committee found that the proposal "substantially undervalues" Wendy's and does not reflect potential gains from the chain's ongoing turnaround strategy, the company said in a press release Thursday.
"Our confidence rests firmly in [CEO] Bob Wright's proven track record of seasoned industry leadership, including restaurant business turnarounds," Art Winkleblack, Wendy's board chair and a member of the independent committee, said in a statement.
Trian declined to comment on Wendy's decision.
To stave off a hostile takeover, Wendy's has adopted a shareholder rights plan — or poison pill — with a one-year duration, as of Wednesday, the company said. Wendy's added that the investor group led by Trian rejected an offer from Wendy's for a standstill agreement that would have paused additional share purchases, adding to Wendy's decision to use a poison pill.
The rejection is the latest in the long-running saga between Peltz and the burger chain, which dates back to an activist campaign he led more than two decades ago. A Peltz firm has even owned Wendy's before. In 2008, his company Triarc, which also owned Arby's, bought Wendy's in a $2.3 billion deal. It later sold Arby's, turning Wendy's into a stand-alone company again.
In 2024, Wendy's named Peltz as chairman emeritus after he spent 17 years on the company's board. Trian executive Peter May and Peltz's son, Bradley, still sit on Wendy's board.
Wendy's also reported its third-quarter results on Thursday. Its same-store sales declined for the seventh straight quarter. However, its quarterly earnings and revenue topped Wall Street's expectations.
Shares of Wendy's fell less than 1% in morning trading. The takeover offer had lifted the stock, which has lost about 60% of its value over the last three years.
Wendy's is not the only restaurant chain that has found itself in the crosshairs of activist investors. Applebee's owner Dine Brands recently adopted a poison pill to block a takeover bid from investment firms Arkhouse Management and Cobblers Cove Capital.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Mobile app technology company AppLovin ( APP ) (NASDAQ:APP) announced better-than-expected revenue in Q3 2026, with revenue up 55.5% year on year to $2.18 billion. In addition, next quarter's revenue guidance ($2.38 billion at the midpoint) was surprisingly strong and 5.5% above analysts' consensus estimates. Its GAAP profit of $4.30 per share was 6.6% above analysts' consensus estimates.
For more on AppLovin, read our full research report .
AppLovin stock rose 18% before the bell on Thursday.
Revenue $2.18 billion vs analysts' consensus estimates of $2.07 billion, according to S&P (55.5% year-on-year growth, 5.4% beat)
EPS (GAAP) $4.30 vs analysts' consensus estimates of $4.03 (6.6% beat)
Adjusted EBITDA $1.84 billion vs analysts' consensus estimates of $1.73 billion (84.3% margin, 6.3% beat)
Revenue guidance $2.38 billion at the midpoint for Q4 2026, above analysts' consensus estimates of $2.25 billion
EBITDA guidance $2.01 billion at the midpoint for Q4 2026, above analysts' consensus estimates of $1.88 billion
Operating margin 78.2%, up from 76.8% in the same quarter last year
Free cash flow margin 64.9%, up from 45.2% in the previous quarter
Market capitalization $82.16 billion
A company's long-term revenue performance is one signal of its overall quality. Any business can have short-term success, but a top-tier one grows for years. AppLovin's revenue grew at a solid 24.8% compounded annual growth rate over the last five years. Its growth surpassed the average software company and shows its offerings resonate with customers.
Long-term growth is the most important, but within software, a half-decade historical view may miss new innovations or demand cycles. AppLovin's annualized revenue growth of 39.2% over the last two years is above its five-year trend, suggesting its demand was strong and recently accelerated.
This quarter, AppLovin reported strong year-on-year revenue growth of 55.5%, and its $2.18 billion of revenue beat Wall Street's consensus estimates by 5.4%. Management is guiding for a 43.6% year-on-year increase in revenue next quarter.
Looking further ahead, sell-side analysts expect revenue to grow 25.8% over the next 12 months, according to S&P, a deceleration versus the last two years. Despite the slowdown, this projection is strong and suggests the market expects success for its products and services.
The customer acquisition cost, or CAC, payback period measures the months a company needs to recoup the money spent on acquiring a new customer. This metric helps assess how quickly a business can break even on its sales and marketing investments.
AppLovin is highly efficient at acquiring new customers, and its CAC payback period was 1.2 months this quarter. The company's rapid recovery of its customer acquisition costs indicates it has a highly differentiated product offering and a strong brand reputation. These dynamics give AppLovin more resources to pursue new product initiatives while maintaining the flexibility to increase its sales and marketing investments.
AppLovin's outlook stood out in a quarter with clear positives: EBITDA guidance for next quarter came in well above analysts' consensus estimates, and revenue guidance also topped Wall Street's consensus. Shares soared 24.9% to $339.10 immediately after the results.
AppLovin had a positive quarter, but one earnings result doesn't necessarily make the stock a buy. Assessing whether it is a good investment requires considering its valuation and business quality, as well as what happened in the latest quarter. articles.title_orig: Wendy's rejects $1.4 billion hostile takeover bid, saying it undervalues the company
articles.title_zh: Wendy's rejects $1.4 billion hostile takeover bid, saying it undervalues the company
articles.content_orig:
Wendy's board of directors on Thursday unanimously rejected a $1.4 billion hostile takeover bid from a group of investment firms, saying the offer undervalues the restaurant chain and is not in the best interest of shareholders.
"The Independent Committee thoroughly evaluated this Proposal and unanimously concluded that it substantially undervalues Wendy's standalone prospects and long-term earnings potential," Art Winkleblack, chairman of the board, said in a statement, while also expressing confidence in CEO Bob Wright.
The takeover bid was led by asset management firm Trian Partners, founded by activist investor Nelson Peltz, along with Flynn Group LP, BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners.
The groups are offering $7.35 per share for Wendy's, whose stock traded at $7.75 before markets opened on Thursday. Wendy's confirmed it received the unsolicited offer last month and said it would create an independent board to review the proposal.
Although it remains profitable, Wendy's has faced slowing revenue growth in recent years, and its stock price has slumped nearly 14% over the last 12 months.
In its latest earnings report on Thursday, Wendy's said that U.S. same-restaurant sales decreased 5.7% in the third quarter, compared with the same period last year. The chain reported $547 million in revenue, down from $549.5 million in the year-ago quarter.
Wendy's is losing traction with customers as inflation and rising beef costs force the burger chain to raise prices, the Associated Press reported last week.
The company has also struggled with operational issues, including staffing, employee training, handling drive-thru orders and marketing, Wright said during a call with Wall Street analysts in August. More broadly, he acknowledged that Wendy's must improve the quality of its food to drive business.
"Wendy's has always been known for quality, fresh, never frozen beef, hamburgers made to order, bacon cooked in our restaurants and fresh produce prepared daily," he said. "But over time, we've drifted away from some of the standards that made Wendy's distinctive. While we've maintained core practices in some areas, we've led cost and efficiency drive decisions that weaken that differentiation."
Other businesses across the fast-food industry are also struggling as inflation weighs on customers' wallets. McDonald's reported on Wednesday that it would offer a new array of affordable options next year to boost sales.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Rotation Away From AI Stocks Increases as Money Flows to AI Landlords - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Rotation Away From AI Stocks Increases as Money Flows to AI Landlords - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 looks flat before the bell, but a split is tearing through the market. After voters took aim at data centers, one group of AI winners is surging while the companies that supply them slide. The Fed speaks…
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
The S&P 500 is headed for a near-flat start Thursday. As of about 8:20 a.m. ET, funds that track the index were up 0.1% before the bell. Under that calm number, the S&P 500 is splitting in two. Hyperscalers and Apple ( NASDAQ:AAPL | AAPL Price Prediction ) are adding to Wednesday’s post-election rally, while chipmakers are falling on concerns that voters just made AI data centers harder to build. The biggest scheduled event of the day is the Federal Reserve’s policy statement at 2 p.m. ET.
On Tuesday, Democrats flipped both the House and Senate. Voters also sided against AI data centers in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, according to CNBC . Investors took that to mean the AI expansion will be slower and more expensive. That outcome helps the companies that already own data centers and hurts the ones selling them chips.
Amazon ( NASDAQ:AMZN ) jumped 8% Wednesday and is up another 2% premarket. Apple rose nearly 7% Wednesday and is adding 1%.
Apple trades near $354. Because the Dow is price-weighted, a stock with a share price that high has extra pull on the index. This is why the Dow leads this morning.
NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) is down 2% premarket, adding to an 18% drop over the past month. Intel ( NASDAQ:INTC ) is off 3% and has lost 51% in a month.
The leveraged Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X ETF ( NYSEARCA:SOXL ) is indicated down 11%. The fund resets every day to deliver triple the chip index’s move, so losses pile up fast when chips keep falling.
While the Dow rises, the Nasdaq-100 proxy is falling. That gap shows money moving away from chip suppliers and toward blue chips and companies that already own AI capacity (we featured seven suppliers behind the data center expansion, from power to cooling, in a free report you can grab here ). Needham analyst Laura Martin summed it up: “Hyperscalers are AI incumbents.” Siebert Financial’s Mark Malek pointed to where the risk lies: “The most vulnerable AI companies are the borrowers, not necessarily the biggest spenders.”
Wall Street’s concerns gauge, the VIX, is almost 21. That puts it in elevated territory, up 3 points from a week earlier. The 10-year Treasury yield is just under 5%, which keeps borrowing costs high for the rate-sensitive small caps in the Russell 2000.
The top of the Fed’s target range is 4% going into today’s announcement. Any hint about future rate cuts will likely move small caps and high-valuation tech the most. articles.title_orig: James Carville Tells Trump His Misery Is Only Just Beginning
articles.title_zh: James Carville Tells Trump His Misery Is Only Just Beginning
articles.content_orig:
Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville predicted that President Donald Trumpâs life is going to get far worse after Democrats seized control of Congress in their midterm landslide.
âIf you listen to me, President Trump, youâre probably not, but somebody is. Itâs going to get worse. Youâre going to get more depressed,â said Carville, in an appearance Wednesday on the Politicon podcast with Al Hunt.
In the interview, Carville urged the new Democratic crop of lawmakers elected to House and Senate majorities to send a clear anti-corruption message, for example, by banning stock trading by members of Congress. âCorruption is for good reason becom[ing] front and center here,â he said.
James Talarico supporters celebrate on an historic night in Texas.
Polls ahead of the midterms showed government corruption was among votersâ key concerns, with 89 percent of respondents in a September Gallup poll saying they believed it was widespread.
Despite Trump holding veto power over any new legislation passed by the Democratic Congress, Carville said the party could do real damage to the president by putting the issue firmly in the spotlight.
By clicking â SUBSCRIBE â you agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy .
âYou can have intensive, rigorous investigations, and at the same time, pass legislation [that] may not be enacted in the law. You then set an agenda,â he said.
Carville pointed to âhow much they [Democrats] can do in terms of bringing to light all of the corruption thatâs taken place, and I think theyâre going to do that.â
Carville also said the results had exposed divisions in the GOP, with Vice President JD Vance in a post on X Wednesda y appearing to criticize his bossâs election strategy and the war with Iran that proved another key factor in the Republican defeat.
âI think the tension with Vance in the White House is going to get greater, and it was a bad night for Republicans,â said Carville.
Vance is at his core a skeptic of U.S. military intervention in the Middle East.
Carville masterminded President Bill Clintonâs election victories in the 1990s, and has long been an adamant critic of Donald Trump.
On the eve of the midterms, he predicted a Republican wipeout. In an appearance on MS NOW , he said he believed the economy and allegations of corruption against Trump and his inner circle would decide the vote.
âI think people have tied corruption to the economy, so I want to be very clear. Corruption is a challenge, and every election is about the economy. It always has been. But I think the corruption issue is really kind of center stage,â he said.

articles.title_orig: Why Trump's midterm blues mean short-term gain, long-term pain for China
articles.title_zh: Why Trump's midterm blues mean short-term gain, long-term pain for China
articles.content_orig:
Democratic victories and opposition to AI infrastructure highlight concerns over power bills, water use and the impact on local communities
Strong voter backlash in the US midterm elections against AI infrastructure projects, including data centres, indicates that framing the domestic buildout as key to competing with China failed to convince Americans and underscores the need to address local concerns, according to analysts.
“The argument that we need to build more data centres to win in AI against China no longer seems to have the kind of resonance it did before, if it ever did, frankly,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Centre.
Lizzi Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, echoed that assessment, saying: “The lesson is that invoking China as a justification for tech and industrial investment is becoming less effective.”

articles.title_orig: China’s Yutong Bus expands overseas as new-energy bus exports surge
articles.title_zh: China’s Yutong Bus expands overseas as new-energy bus exports surge
articles.content_orig:
‘Overseas public transport demand is growing fast, and international buyers are seeking more premium electric buses,’ Asia-Pacific CEO says
China’s Yutong Bus, the world’s largest electric bus manufacturer, is seeing its overseas shipments climb steadily, with demand growing rapidly in countries such as Australia, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia and Morocco.
Based in Zhengzhou in central China’s Henan province, the company now generates more than half of its total revenue from overseas sales. New-energy models – comprising pure-electric and hybrid vehicles – have made up 25 per cent of its bus exports so far this year, a sharp increase from just 3 per cent in 2018.
Yutong holds more than 10 per cent of the global market, including China, for large and medium-sized buses and coaches, according to the company. Its competitors include domestic peers BYD, Zhongtong Bus and Xiamen King Long United Automotive Industry, as well as overseas companies like Mercedes-Benz and Volvo.

Wang Ning joins predecessors in disgrace as Beijing deepens scrutiny of internal security
A former commander of China’s paramilitary force has been stripped of his senior political advisory roles, sealing a sweep of more than 15 years in which three consecutive heads of the People’s Armed Police have fallen from grace.
The top political advisory body revoked his membership during its closing session, which was presided over by China’s fourth-ranking leader and chair of the CPPCC, Wang Huning, according to Xinhua.
China keeps most investigations within its military secret. Consequently, notices announcing the removal of retired generals from China’s national legislative and political advisory bodies have become an important channel for observing the latest moves.

articles.title_orig: Live: France braces for nationwide strikes in fresh test for Macron’s policies
articles.title_zh: Live: France braces for nationwide strikes in fresh test for Macron’s policies
articles.content_orig:
Hospital workers, air traffic and rail staff expected to join strikes amid renewed protests over education and rising living costs
Hundreds of thousands are expected to march in demonstrations across France as trade unions call for a nationwide strike expected to extend to hospital workers, air traffic control, the post office, teachers and rail staff.
President Emmanuel Macron’s final months in office continue to be marred by domestic crises, as high school students protesting over poor teaching conditions have been joined by workers in weekly protests over the cost of living. Meanwhile, the government is struggling to pass a belt-tightening budget in a divided parliament as public debt approaches 120% of economic output.
Ahead of Thursday’s strike action, France’s four main rail unions said that the government’s proposed budget cuts would “worsen poverty, slash social security, freeze state workers’ salaries and dry up investment needed for environmental measures”.
Amid the renewed protests centred on living costs, public spending cuts and the troubled education system, the far-right, anti-immigration candidate Marine Le Pen is polling high for the 2027 presidential election to replace Macron next spring.
High school students continued to blockade schools over overcrowded classes and dilapidated buildings, saying the government’s proposed measures on capping some class sizes and loaning funds to regional authorities to fix schools were not enough. University students joined in blockading some faculties. Trade unions from across the political landscape joined in a call for strikes over the rising cost of living, with private schools’ teachers unions also joining strikes alongside state school teachers.
Rights’ groups protested over what they said was heavy policing and an “authoritarian” attempt by Macron’s executive to clamp down on the right to demonstrate.
The French Human Rights League said there was an “authoritarian shift” to stifle “any dissenting voice” as the government put in place heavy policing and authorities issued restrictions on demonstrating in city centres, as well as curfews in certain areas.
Sophie Binet, the head of the leftwing CGT union, said: “We’re living at a very serious time with a very dangerous authoritarian drift from the government”, criticising decisions by authorities in cities such as Rennes, Toulouse and Lyon to push demonstrations out of city centres.

Marylise Léon, the head of the moderate CFDT trade union, said: “The principle of a demonstration is its visibility.”
The national rail operator SNCF said there would be “disturbances” to train services on regional lines and some parts of the greater Paris area. Dockers said there would be disruption in French ports. The education ministry said it expected almost 18% of nursery and primary school teachers to strike. Trade unions said they also expected secondary teachers to take part in Thursday’s strike.

articles.title_orig: How India Can Manage Chinese Surpluses
articles.title_zh: How India Can Manage Chinese Surpluses
articles.content_orig:
By Thomas Asplund-Meineckem , William B. Smith, and  Shiro Armstrong
China’s resurgent trade surplus has revived fears across developing Asia that it is pulling up the ladder of export-led industrialization behind it. In New Delhi, India’s bilateral trade deficit with China — over $112 billion in 2025–26 — is being read as the result of unfair Chinese competition and domestic structural weakness, both cited as grounds for protection. But viewing China primarily as a competitor misses its potentially complementary role and the case for managing the relationship rather than retreating from it.
Concerns over a ‘China squeeze’ hold that China has industrialized without ceding labor-intensive industries, partly due to its industrial policies and structurally undervalued renminbi. The argument goes that Chinese goods undercut developing countries’ firms at home and outcompete them in third markets, while China demands few of their exports, leaving developing countries little room to industrialize.
New Delhi has been especially receptive to this argument, framing economic engagement with China as a threat to be contained. In thinly veiled comments directed at China in June 2026, Minister of External Affairs Subrahmanyam Jaishankar argued that ‘the right to industrialize, indeed the capacity to do so, is being denied’ to many developing countries.
Convinced that its firms cannot compete with China on fair terms, New Delhi has turned its trade policy inwards . India has increased tariffs since 2018 to an average of around 17.6 percent, among the highest in Asia, and raised non-tariff barriers. In November 2019, India also walked out of Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) negotiations, largely over concerns it would expose Indian firms and farmers to a surge of cheap Chinese imports. But this ‘ RCEP minus China ’ strategy leaves India outside the regional production networks deeply integrated with China.
Underlying this strategy is concern about India’s bilateral trade deficit. But economies tend to run deficits with countries that supply their inputs and surpluses with those that buy their outputs. Imports of this kind reflect complementarities between economies, and by lowering costs, make local firms more productive and competitive.
China is above all a supplier to Indian manufacturing. Capital goods, machinery and intermediate goods accounted for around 87 percent of Indian imports from China in 2024.
India’s pharmaceutical and electronics industries show the value of integration into Chinese value chains. Between 2015 and 2022, Indian value added in electronics exports nearly tripled as their Chinese content rose sixfold. In pharmaceuticals, it rose by half as Chinese content doubled.
Labor-intensive industries like textiles show a similar pattern. With China moving upstream out of garment assembly, Bangladesh and Vietnam have taken substantial market share. But India’s share of global textile exports has remained stagnant at around 3 percent , with its garment makers paying higher duties on imported fabric.
Tariff and non-tariff barriers to Chinese inputs shelter upstream firms but raise costs for downstream exporters who compete with Chinese exports in foreign markets regardless. Input tariff neutrality would help Indian firms integrate into global value chains, raising domestic value added in absolute terms even if the foreign value-added share of exports rises.
Deeper integration would also help India sell more to China. Despite supplying almost 17 percent of India’s imports in 2025–26, China bought only 4.4 percent of India’s exports. Part of the gap reflects Chinese barriers in key Indian sectors, but Indian firms also struggle to match Chinese rivals on cost and scale.
Indian protectionism against China will not resolve the distortions imposed by Chinese overcapacity . At best, India’s barriers offset some of their effects — but raise costs for Indian firms. India can gain more from importing cheaper Chinese equipment, green technology and productive capacity for its own industrialization — especially given unilateral action will not change the policies driving China’s surpluses.
Genuine Chinese distortions demand a collective response through international and regional agreements. RCEP’s joint committees and ministerial meetings allow members to press Beijing on unfair practices, and its standards and customs chapters provide channels to raise the approval delays preventing Indian goods from reaching Chinese markets.
Membership would also pull India into regional production networks. RCEP’s common rules of origin make it easier to spread production across member economies, since inputs from any member count towards origin, qualifying the final good for preferential tariffs across the bloc. RCEP also provides safeguards against damaging import surges, allowing members to suspend tariff cuts or raise duties when imports injure domestic industries.
RCEP members remain open to India’s accession — New Delhi could take up an observer seat now and apply to join without the waiting period other applicants face. The agreement’s first General Review in 2027 offers a natural moment to negotiate entry.
The Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) offers further avenues for managing Chinese surpluses. China’s application to join — pending since September 2021 — offers the region leverage, holding out access to CPTPP markets in return for reform of state-owned enterprises, investment and government procurement.
The same logic applies to India, for which CPTPP membership is a longer-term goal. Its regulatory disciplines would demand reforms India’s political economy has long resisted. A staged process — beginning with a gap analysis and cooperation in less contentious areas before negotiating transition periods and carve-outs for sensitive sectors — would give policymakers time to build domestic support for reform.
Indian policymakers should understand China not only as a competitor but as a potential complementor. The trade deficit driving India inwards largely consists of inputs that make its firms more productive and competitive. Unilateral protection and absence from RCEP and CPTPP leave India outside the production networks that would allow its manufacturing sector to prosper, and without a voice to press genuine concerns. Managing the relationship through regional arrangements offers a surer way up the ladder of export-led industrialization than going it alone.
Thomas Asplund-Meinecke is Project Assistant at the East Asian Bureau of Economic Research, Crawford School of Public Policy, The Australian National University.
William B Smith is Project Assistant at the East Asian Bureau of Economic Research, Crawford School of Public Policy, The Australian National University.
Shiro Armstrong is Professor and Director of the Australia-Japan Research Center in the Crawford School of Public Policy, The Australian National University.

articles.title_orig: Russia, China may be more aggressive if they feel Trump is on "his way out": Brookings
articles.title_zh: Russia, China may be more aggressive if they feel Trump is on "his way out": Brookings
articles.content_orig:
Russia and China could become more aggressive over the next two years if they conclude that President Donald Trump is politically weakened and on "his way out" after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, Brookings Institution senior fellow Robert Kagan told CNBC.
Speaking on " Squawk Box Asia ," Kagan said the war with Iran had also exposed how Washington has "proved itself rather incapable militarily" in terms of capacity, which would be critical in Asia.
"Everybody can see how much our stocks are depleted in terms of interceptors and missiles, which are of vital interest in the Asian theater," he said.
Congressional Budget Office reports have estimated that the conflict depleted as much as two-thirds of U.S. missile-defense interceptors since June 2025, largely because of efforts to defend Israel against Iranian attacks. This could leave the U.S. with constrained inventories for several years.
Kagan said the deployment of three U.S. aircraft carriers to the Middle East had reduced the U.S. naval presence available in Asia, potentially giving China more room to act assertively in the region.
"I think Trump's only interest right now is in cutting economic deals with China. I don't think he has any real interest in confronting China, but that is going to lead China to be even more aggressive," he said.
In December, Trump approved an $11 billion arms package for Taiwan, but later held back on a second package worth about $14 billion, calling it a "bargaining chip" in talks with China.
China claims self-governing Taiwan as its territory. While Washington does not have a mutual defense treaty with the island, U.S. law requires it to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself.
Former CIA Director William Burns said in 2023 that Chinese President Xi Jinping had instructed the military to be ready to invade Taiwan by 2027, while stressing that this did not mean Xi had decided to launch an invasion that year or at all.
Kagan's comments come as U.S., China and Russia discuss a possible trilateral summit between Trump, Xi and President Vladimir Putin at the APEC Leaders' meeting in Shenzhen later this month.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Wednesday that Beijing was "in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state," although no agenda has been announced.
Putin had reportedly floated the idea of a three-way summit with Trump and Xi in October to discuss ending the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table.
"If it's clear that Donald Trump is on his way out, and the United States may be returning to something like normal, I don't want to overstate that, but they may feel both of them, both Russia and China, may feel that the time to move is in the next two years," Kagan said.
